items.title: Residents of North Darfur village urge reopening of school closed since war began
items.summary: Residents of Al-Mudayib village in Sudan’s North Darfur State have appealed to the relevant authorities The post Residents of North Darfur village urge reopening of school closed since war began appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: Residents of Al-Mudayib village in Sudan’s North Darfur State have appealed to the relevant authorities to reopen the area’s only school, which has been closed since the war began in April 2023. Ibrahim Ahmed Al-Doudo, chairperson of the school’s education council, told Radio Tamazuj on Tuesday that the school had not reopened since fighting broke out. Three of its six classrooms need to be rebuilt, while accommodation for teachers also needs to be constructed, he said. The school had 654 pupils, both boys and girls, before the war, Al-Doudo said. They have now been out of school for more than three years. Several university graduates from the area have offered to volunteer as teachers if the school reopens, he said. The school also lacks desks, textbooks and other educational materials, while funds are needed to support volunteer teachers, Al-Doudo said. Tribo Burma Yousif, a resident of Al-Mudayib, said the closure had severely affected the community and urged authorities, donors and other well-wishers to help restore the school. He said traditional Quranic schools in the area had also been forced to close or damaged because of the conflict. Al-Mudayib School, established in 1994, was originally known as Al-Mudayib Mixed Basic School and had eight classrooms. Its capacity was later reduced to six classrooms following Sudan’s education reforms, which introduced a six-year primary cycle followed by three years each of intermediate and secondary education. The school is in the Mustariha administrative unit of Al-Waha locality in North Darfur state. Mustariha was the stronghold of tribal leader Musa Hilal, who had declared his support for the Sudanese army. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) attacked the area in February, taking control after fighting with forces aligned with Hilal and prompting the displacement of thousands of residents. The conflict between Sudan’s army and the RSF began in April 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions, according to the United Nations and aid agencies. The war has also severely disrupted education, with schools destroyed, damaged or used for other purposes and millions of children deprived of regular schooling. The post Residents of North Darfur village urge reopening of school closed since war began appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.title: South Darfur: University of Nyala prepares to resume in-person classes
items.summary: A campaign to rehabilitate the University of Nyala has begun in the capital of Sudan’s The post South Darfur: University of Nyala prepares to resume in-person classes appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: A campaign to rehabilitate the University of Nyala has begun in the capital of Sudan’s South Darfur state, as authorities prepare to resume in-person classes after years of disruption caused by the war. The work includes repairing and refurbishing classrooms, faculty buildings and administrative offices, officials overseeing the campaign said. Mohamed Hassan Al-Taayshi, prime minister of the Tasees government, visited the university to inspect the rehabilitation work and review its progress. The Tasees government, an RSF-aligned administration known as the Government of Peace and Unity, is headquartered in Nyala. Al-Taayshi said universities in areas controlled by the Tasees government had sufficient capacity to accommodate students. Where capacity was insufficient, authorities would resort to online education using internet services. The prime minister also praised residents for protecting the University of Nyala from destruction and vandalism during the war. Al-Noor Ali Ahmed Fadl, head of the popular committee overseeing the campaign, thanked Al-Taayshi for his support, saying it had helped overcome obstacles facing the rehabilitation effort. Higher Education Minister Eid Ibrahim Breima said classes would initially resume in person before later shifting to online learning. He said the government planned in the next phase to share the cost of higher education with the public, with greater emphasis on applied fields such as engineering, medicine and agriculture to help develop a skilled workforce. Sudan’s war erupted on April 15, 2023, when fighting broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict has displaced more than 14 million people, according to the United Nations. The RSF controls most of Darfur, including Nyala, while the army holds large areas of eastern and central Sudan. Millions of Sudanese have fled their homes, with many crossing into neighbouring countries including Chad, Egypt and South Sudan. The post South Darfur: University of Nyala prepares to resume in-person classes appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.title: Leaked files shed new light on Sudan Army’s alleged chemical weapons program
items.summary: The SAF has found itself at the center of a major crisis following news investigations by leading U.S. media outlets that exposed its involvement in developing and deploying chemical weapons. The post Leaked files shed new light on Sudan Army’s alleged chemical weapons program appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have found themselves at the center of a major crisis following news investigations by leading U.S. media outlets that exposed their involvement in developing and deploying chemical weapons in the ongoing conflict against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Mohsin Osman reports. On Saturday, The New York Times and The Washington Post published dual investigative reports based on leaked intelligence materials. The files include approximately 150 documents, photographs, video clips, and intercepted communications, alongside thousands of text messages retrieved from the phones of Sudanese officers. The evidence points to an alleged program established in 2024 to manufacture chlorine-based munitions. It details bomb design blueprints, testing operations, and a coordinated cover-up strategy initiated after the plot was uncovered by the United States. The records also outline plans to siphon chlorine gas from a civilian water treatment facility that had originally received the chemical from international aid agencies. These revelations reignite long-standing allegations of chemical weapons usage that have shadowed SAF leadership since last year, significantly heightening international pressure on the military command. The United States previously imposed sanctions on Sudan in May 2025 over allegations that the military deployed chemical weapons during the conflict in 2024. The sanctions took effect on July 20, 2025. Authorities in Port Sudan have consistently rejected these accusations, maintaining that they do not produce, stockpile, or use chemical weapons, and emphasizing their adherence to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). A Covert Program Amid Escalating Pressure According to The New York Times, the SAF turned to chemical weapons early in 2024 to break a strategic stalemate, as RSF fighters held firm control over most of the capital, Khartoum. Leaked records show that Brigadier General Tariq Hussein emerged as a central figure in July 2024, orchestrating the design, planning, and execution of the program. Intercepted messages reveal that Hussein proposed using chlorine to give army forces a tactical edge in the battle for Khartoum. He distributed prototype schematics for an explosive warhead integrated with roughly 33 pounds of chlorine gas, with production commencing that same month. In messages published by the Times, Hussein noted that the hybrid munitions were designed to maximize lethality—either by shrapnel fragmentation or chlorine gas poisoning—asserting that the explosion would destroy all chemical traces of the attack. On July 22, an Antonov cargo plane took off from Merowe Airport, roughly 200 miles north of Khartoum, to conduct a test launch. Following the trial, Hussein reported that the experiment was a “100 percent success,” attaching a video of a desert explosion and confirming that the munition “hit the target and released the gas.” Brigadier General Amir Idris, identified in records as the supervisor of military drone operations, responded with a single directive: “Top Secret.” Technical Hazards and Signs of Lethality The communications reveal that the program faced severe technical flaws. Chemical leaks were a recurring issue; on one occasion, workers found dead insects and scorpions on the floor of a hangar after overnight exposure to leaking gas. The incident underscored the volatile nature of the agent being handled long before it reached the battlefield. Concurrently, the program faced a critical challenge in securing a steady supply of chlorine. Diverting Humanitarian Chlorine Supplies According to The New York Times, 20 cylinders of chlorine gas were smuggled across the border from a neighboring country in late August 2024. Hussein calculated that this batch would yield roughly 1,100 bombs. Hussein subsequently sought internal sources, turning to local civilian infrastructure in violation of international norms. He admitted to sourcing additional chlorine from the Al-Manara water treatment plant in Omdurman—one of the few remaining operational facilities amid the war. “Al-Manara has some of those cylinders, and we took them from there,” Hussein stated in an August 26 voice message to Idris. The diversion of these supplies carries significant gravity, as the chlorine at the plant was intended for emergency water purification during cholera outbreaks rather than military application. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) confirmed to the Times that it had donated 30 chlorine cylinders to the plant in 2023, while CARE reported delivering 35 cylinders across 2024 and 2025. A UNICEF spokesperson added that the organization supplied chlorine to six treatment plants in Khartoum, including Al-Manara, between 2023 and 2025. By October 2024, Hussein reported manufacturing approximately 300 chemical munitions, most of which were stored at Merowe Airport. Earlier in September, Hussein sent a notable message to a colleague stating, “They drank the gas,” describing an attack on RSF fighters at the Al-Jaili oil refinery north of Khartoum. This account aligns with claims made by the RSF on September 13, when the paramilitary group issued a statement accusing the army of firing “toxic” missiles at the refinery. Footage circulated online at the time showed men in civilian clothing inside the facility wearing oxygen masks. Command Responsibility and Cover-Up Efforts The New York Times indicates that the program was likely shuttered once U.S. officials detected its existence and moved to apply targeted sanctions. Intercepted communications reveal that the head of Sudan’s Armed Forces, General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, instructed Hussein to “erase all traces” of the operation. The response was: “The operation was completed a month ago.” During a subsequent round of measures in June, the U.S. sanctioned Hussein for importing explosives for bomb production, though that specific designation did not explicitly cite chemical weapons. By that time, Burhan had established an internal committee to investigate the U.S. allegations. According to documents in the file, Hussein himself—the architect of the program—was appointed as an advisor to the panel. The intelligence indicates that General Burhan was not merely informed after the fact, but was directly involved in overseeing the chemical weapons program. His direct knowledge was a primary factor in the U.S. decision to impose sanctions on him in January 2025. While proving chemical weapons usage in conflict zones remains complex, arms experts consulted by The New York Times concurred that available evidence strongly points to their deployment in the Sudanese conflict. However, they stressed the necessity of an independent field investigation. Addressing the findings, the Emergency Lawyers group, a Sudanese legal advocacy organization, issued a statement calling for a transparent international probe. The group urged that “international experts be granted safe, unconditional access to targeted sites, enable the physical examination of munitions fragments and delivery systems, and be permitted to interview witnesses and victims independently and securely.” The post Leaked files shed new light on Sudan Army’s alleged chemical weapons program appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

Over recent months, I have spoken with several American diplomats in Mogadishu, Nairobi, New York, Washington and elsewhere […] The post As Justin Davis Le
items.body: As Justin Davis concludes his tenure as Chargé d’Affaires at the United States Embassy in Mogadishu, he leaves at a time when the relationship between Somalia and the U.S.is changing, perhaps more significantly than official statements suggest. Over recent months, I have spoken with several American diplomats in Mogadishu, Nairobi, New York, Washington and elsewhere about where the U.S. now stands on Somalia. Some are serving officials, while others know the Somalia file closely. They did not agree on everything and some were more candid than others, but the conversations repeatedly came back to the same question: how much responsibility are Somalis themselves prepared to take for the future of their country? Davis has run the US Embassy through a particularly difficult period. Politics in Washington changed sharply as “America First” came to define the administration’s approach abroad. In Somalia, political divisions deepened, relations between the Federal Government and some Federal Member States deteriorated and Al-Shabaab and Daesh continued to pose serious security threats. At the same time, competition among foreign powers for influence in Somalia and the wider Horn of Africa intensified. One American diplomat described Davis’s challenge to me as finding a way to reconcile “America First” with “Somalia First”. When I asked what “Somalia First” meant, the answer was strikingly straightforward: Somalia for Somalis, strong Somali institutions and political leaders taking responsibility for their own country. Several diplomats worried that foreign interests had become too entangled with Somalia’s domestic political competition and that Somali politicians were themselves sometimes opening the door to that interference. “Somalia’s future is not for sale,” one diplomat told me. It was not an argument for Somalia to turn away from international partners. The country needs them and none of the Americans I spoke with disputed that. Their concern was that Somalia cannot insist on its sovereignty while allowing domestic political disputes to become entangled with competing foreign agendas. In their view, Somali politicians have to find ways of settling their differences without constantly looking towards foreign capitals. Another diplomat was equally direct. “Somalia is not a child. Somalia is a partner,” he said. America was prepared to cooperate with Somalia and support it, but the relationship had to be one between partners, with Somalia taking responsibility for its own choices and future. Under the current US policy, American interests in Somalia have become narrower and more clearly defined. Three priorities came up repeatedly in my conversations: counterterrorism, law enforcement cooperation and immigration coordination. These are increasingly the hard interests around which Washington is organising its relationship with Mogadishu. But the American assessment of Somalia was far from entirely negative. Diplomats acknowledged good progress in law enforcement cooperation and immigration coordination and spoke positively about the working relationship with Somali authorities in these areas. They also recognised that Mogadishu is considerably more peaceful than it was before, something several of them regarded as an important achievement that should not be overlooked. Their frustration was much greater when the conversation moved beyond Mogadishu. American diplomats were unhappy with the pace of counter-offensive operations against Al-Shabaab outside the capital. They had expected greater movement and more sustained gains on the ground. Their concern was not simply about launching military operations but whether those operations were producing lasting results and maintaining sufficient pressure on Al-Shabaab. Politics inevitably entered that discussion. Several diplomats believed the prolonged confrontation between the federal government, federal member states and opposition politicians was taking attention away from the security campaign. To them, political cohesion and the fight against Al-Shabaab are not separate issues. A country whose political leaders are consumed by disputes among themselves will inevitably find it more difficult to sustain a coherent national security effort. The reduction in American humanitarian and development assistance also reflects the wider change in Washington. One diplomat pushed back when I described this as a retreat from humanitarian engagement. He preferred to call it a “reorganisation of assistance”, with more emphasis on priorities, accountability and results. Others were more candid in acknowledging that America’s broader interest in Somalia had declined and that Washington was reconsidering how much money and political attention it was prepared to commit. Some also admitted that Washington itself had spent several years struggling to decide exactly what its overriding national security interests in Somalia were. Over time, American engagement had expanded into counterterrorism, security assistance, humanitarian relief, state-building, democratisation and political mediation. The current approach is much less expansive. The message now is simpler: America will help Somalia, but Somalia must also help itself. That view becomes particularly clear when American diplomats talk about Somali politics. They see fragmentation on almost every side. Within the federal government, the executive, parliament and other state institutions appear increasingly aligned. Yet relations between Mogadishu and important Federal Member States remain badly fractured, particularly with Puntland and Jubaland. The Americans are not putting all the blame on Villa Somalia. They are also critical of the opposition. Several diplomats, in separate conversations, used exactly the same word to describe it: “fragmented”. They questioned how much opposition leaders trust one another and whether their alliances are built around a common political programme or simply the convenience of opposing the current leadership. One diplomat posed a difficult question: if opposition to one administration is what brings everyone together, what happens when that administration is no longer there? What struck me during these conversations was that the Americans were rarely questioning the competence of Somalis themselves. They spoke about capable politicians, professionals, entrepreneurs, civil society leaders and a remarkably resilient population. Their frustration was that all this talent had still not produced enough political cohesion around a minimum national interest. One senior diplomat used the U.S. itself as an example. He spoke about “American exceptionalism”, not to suggest that American politicians agree with one another, but almost to make the opposite point. American politics can be bitterly divided, he said, yet there remains a sense of national identity and certain interests around which Americans can still rally. His question was: what is the Somali equivalent? Curiously, the Americans saw a glimpse of an answer in the controversy involving Somalia’s renowned referee Omar Artan. A senior diplomat told me that when Artan was returned from the U.S. and was not allowed into the country, calls to the US Embassy in Mogadishu were incessant. According to the diplomat, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was among those seeking an explanation. But what fascinated American officials even more was the public reaction that followed. Diplomats in Washington, Mogadishu, Nairobi and elsewhere were closely watching the scenes of large numbers of young Somalis gathering at Mogadishu Stadium. They saw Somalis who would normally find themselves on different sides of political divides rallying around the same issue. It prompted a question among some of those watching: if Somalis could rally together so powerfully around Omar Artan, why could that same sense of national solidarity not be mobilised around Somalia? For some of the diplomats, the episode demonstrated that the national feeling exists. The problem is turning it into a political culture that can survive elections, clan calculations, disputes between governments and the influence of foreign powers. There is an obvious contradiction in some of this American thinking and the diplomats themselves are not unaware of it. For years, the U.S. was one of the most influential external actors in Somali politics. When a serious political crisis erupted, Somali leaders and international partners looked towards Washington. The Americans convened, persuaded, applied pressure and helped push political rivals towards compromise. That America is less visible today. Some Somali politicians and international partners regard this as a weakness in the current American approach. They believe Washington has withdrawn too far from political engagement and that its reduced role has left a vacuum at precisely the wrong time. Their argument is that America still carries political weight that few other countries can m

items.title: University of Khartoum counts cost of Sudan war as 71% of academics remain abroad, infrastructure destroyed
items.summary: More than seven in 10 academics at the University of Khartoum remain outside Sudan, while... The post University of Khartoum counts cost of Sudan war as 71% of academics remain abroad, infrastructure destroyed appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .
items.body: More than seven in 10 academics at the University of Khartoum remain outside Sudan, while the war has destroyed or damaged much of the institution’s infrastructure, threatening plans for a full return to face-to-face teaching. The University of Khartoum has lost more than half of its staff housing and the operational capacity of its lecture halls, laboratories, and hospitals, while more than 90% of its information and communications technology infrastructure has been damaged, according to a new report by the university’s Academic Staff Association. The report, prepared by the association’s Committee to Ensure the Continuity of the Educational Process, says a full and immediate return to face-to-face teaching faces major obstacles, including the absence of large numbers of students and academics, fragile infrastructure, and the incomplete rehabilitation of university facilities. The university administration asked academic staff to return and resume work by 1 August 2026, as part of plans to resume face-to-face teaching for all levels from September and close internal and external teaching and examination centres. However, a survey of 381 staff members found that 71% remained outside Sudan, while 29% were inside the country. Other data shows that the average number of returning staff in departments at one faculty on the Central Campus was about 20%, while the average in the three best-performing departments at a faculty on the Shambat Campus was about 50%. Attendance at the Education Campus reached 68% by 15 August, compared with only 35% at the Faculty of Arts by 23 August. A transitional plan for a full academic year The association warns that an inflexible return could lead the university to lose more academic staff and proposes a transitional plan lasting a full academic year. Among medical students, about 42% are outside Sudan. Only about 54% express confidence in their theoretical knowledge, while more than 75% have major gaps in clinical skills. More than 90% are concerned about clinical training because of shortages of teaching staff and supervisors, and the lack of readiness of medical facilities. At the Faculty of Engineering, data covering 1,351 students shows that more than 50% are refugees or displaced outside Sudan, while 27% live inside Sudan but outside Khartoum State, meaning that 77.8% are not currently in Khartoum. The data also shows that 74.7% of engineering students do not have accommodation in Khartoum after examinations end, while 57% say they are either completely unable to afford travel costs or can only afford them with extreme difficulty. The report warns that closing external examination centres could prevent more than 80% of students from sitting their exams. Student associations have submitted at least 15 memorandums to faculty deans, as well as another to the university’s vice-chancellor, without receiving a response. At the Faculty of Pharmacy, the proportion of admitted students who enrolled was close to 90% before the war, but fell to about 46% for the deferred 2023 intake and 41% for the deferred 2024 intake. At the Faculty of Education, about 73% of students enrolled, despite the number admitted after the war across two intakes being roughly equivalent to the number previously admitted in a single intake. Laboratories completely destroyed Some university assets have sustained damage of up to about 40%, which could be addressed through maintenance and rehabilitation. Damage to other assets exceeds 40%, while some have been damaged so severely that complete replacement would be more appropriate. The Faculty of Science has lost about 12 laboratories, including around seven that have been completely destroyed. The Faculty of Pharmacy and the main examination hall have also sustained severe damage, alongside near-total losses of vehicles, furniture, computers, servers, network systems, and digital assets. Despite the destruction, the university continued online teaching during the war, held six examination sessions, and graduated about 8,000 students. A seventh session was later held in person at university premises in Khartoum, but saw a noticeable absence among students registered to sit the exams. Before the war, the university’s Academic Council approved a system allowing 50% online teaching to address the accumulation of student cohorts. Phased system for academics As part of rehabilitation efforts, the estimated cost of repairing the Baghdad Hall at the Faculty of Medicine is about $130,000, while repairs to the Anis Hall are estimated at about 300m Sudanese pounds. Rehabilitation work has also been carried out at the Faculty of Engineering and several other faculties, with support from graduates and the private sector. The committee proposes a phased participation system for academics over one academic year, divided into three categories: full return, hybrid participation, and remote online work. Under the proposal, academics in the hybrid category would spend between four and six weeks on campus during each semester, while carrying out the remainder of their duties remotely. The university would cover one return air ticket per semester and provide living expenses during their stay. The committee also recommends reopening external centres for a full academic year, adopting blended learning over the same period, and automatically renewing monthly contracts during the transitional year. Those unable to return after the end of the academic year would be allowed to apply for statutory leave in accordance with university regulations. The committee calls for a specialist academic committee on blended learning, as well as a higher committee for rebuilding the university, involving academics, students, and graduates. It also calls for a reconstruction strategy aimed not simply at restoring the university to its pre-war condition, but rebuilding it according to a new vision. The University of Khartoum, whose history dates back to 1902, had about 44,000 undergraduate and intermediate diploma students in 2025, as well as about 10,000 postgraduate students. It employed 5,501 staff, of whom academics accounted for 36% and non-academic employees 64%. The university includes 23 faculties, 12 research institutes, 10 research centres, four university hospitals, and five main campuses. Its housing facilities previously accommodated more than 20% of academic staff and senior employees, while it was linked to about 1,395 cooperating institutions through academic and research partnerships and agreements. Note: This report has been translated from Arabic with the assistance of artificial intelligence tools, and subsequently reviewed and adapted by a human editor before publication. items.title: Somalia president’s policies have failed the country, says academic
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A prominent Somali professor has issued a sharp public rebuke of Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, warning that his administration’s policies have failed the country and accusing him of presiding over a political collapse that is pushing Somalis back toward tribal and regional allegiances. Afyare Elmi delivered the warning in an open […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A prominent Somali professor has issued a sharp public rebuke of Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, warning that his administration’s policies have failed the country and accusing him of presiding over a political collapse that is pushing Somalis back toward tribal and regional allegiances. Afyare Elmi delivered the warning in an open letter posted to X on Monday, framing it as a direct appeal to the president to change course before, in his words, the country falls apart. “Almost a Full House” in 2022 Elmi opened his letter by recalling the breadth of political support present at Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s inauguration in the Halane area of Mogadishu. “On May 16, 2022, you assumed power with an almost full house. Only Somaliland, which has been seeking international recognition, and the extremist groups, which have been fighting the government, were not in the Halane tent. The rest were present at your inauguration,” Elmi wrote. That coalition, he said, has since collapsed. A Coalition in Retreat “Fast forward to today: the institutions are out of mandate, and you have lost many of the people and groups that were in the Halane tent in 2022,” Elmi wrote, adding that most of the politicians who backed the president’s 2022 victory — including figures from the national opposition, Puntland and Jubaland — are no longer part of the government. He pointed to specific flashpoints across the federal map: Southwest State is experiencing violent conflict, which Elmi attributed to “a poorly conceived and executed transition.” The principle of “do no harm,” which he described as foundational, has “been violated in a big way.” Galmudug and Hirshabelle are, in his words, “ticking time bombs that could explode in any direction.” “Mr. President, your policies have failed the country, and as a result, Somalis are now aligning with regional geopolitics along tribal and regional lines,” Elmi wrote. Elmi’s Prescription: Talks, Not Rhetoric Elmi argued that the way out of the crisis is for the president to recognize the danger the country faces and adopt what he called a pragmatic approach to resolving outstanding disputes “before it is too late.” He said the minimum the Somali public should expect is a credible and competitive political process open to all the actors who were present in 2022. “The time for empty rhetoric and gerrymandering or power-grabbing is over,” he wrote. “It is time to reach a political agreement with the opposition and reconcile with your opponents, both at the state and national levels. You must also return to the dispensation processes that Somalis have known and relied upon in the past.” He closed with a stark warning: “Otherwise, Somalia risks disintegration under your leadership, and such a legacy would be an unbearable burden to bear.” The letter lands as Somalia is contending in real time with escalating political disputes between the federal government in Mogadishu, several regional state administrations, and clan constituencies across the country. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com

items.title: Foreign support for RSF major reason Sudan war persists: Sudan’s prosecutor general
items.summary: Intisar Ahmed Abdelaal calls for ‘decisive measures’ to halt external support for paramilitary group
items.body:
External support for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) is a major reason for the prolonged war and continued violations in Sudan, the country’s prosecutor general said Monday, calling for decisive action to halt it.

Intisar Ahmed Abdelaal made the remarks during a briefing to the UN Human Rights Council’s interactive dialogue on Sudan as part of its 63rd session in Geneva, according to the Sudanese News Agency.

Abdelaal also chairs Sudan’s National Committee for Investigating Crimes and Violations of National and International Law.

“External support for the militia represents a major reason for the prolongation of the war and the continuation of violations,” she said, referring to the RSF.

She urged the council to condemn the support and take “decisive measures” to stop it.

Abdelaal renewed her call for the Human Rights Council and other UN mechanisms to support the national committee, uphold the principle of complementarity, and take immediate steps to end foreign support for the RSF.

She also reaffirmed Sudan’s rejection of external mechanisms that bypass national efforts and reiterated its opposition to the resolution establishing the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for Sudan.

On Thursday, the UN fact-finding mission said external support networks are helping fuel the war in Sudan.

The Sudanese army and the RSF have been fighting since April 2023 in a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

items.title: Sierra Leone ex-president Koroma returns after treason case dropped
items.summary: Former Sierra Leone president Ernest Bai Koroma returned to his home country Sunday, where authorities welcomed him after treason charges against him over an alleged coup attempt were dropped
items.body:
Former Sierra Leone president Ernest Bai Koroma returned to his home country Sunday, where authorities welcomed him after treason charges against him over an alleged coup attempt were dropped.

Koroma had left for Nigeria in 2024, days after being charged with treason and other offences over a deadly 2023 army uprising.

The ex-president, who led Sierra Leone from 2007 to 2018, arrived at the international airport in the capital, Freetown, accompanied by Nigerian ex-president Olusegun Obasanjo and Nigerian Foreign Minister Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, an AFP journalist said.

He was welcomed by Sierra Leone's Foreign Minister Mohamed Rahman Swarray and officials from Koroma's party, the opposition All People's Congress (APC).

"Today I have come back home and I'm happy," Koroma told journalists, smiling.

Koroma had been cleared by Sierra Leonean authorities to travel to Nigeria for three months for medical treatment, but ended up staying more than two years.

In July, Sierra Leone's justice ministry said it had dropped the charges against him, without giving a reason.

On Friday, Vice President Mohamed Jukdeh Jalloh told a gathering of local leaders and residents in Koroma's stronghold, the central city of Makeni, that the ex-leader was returning home.

His homecoming comes ahead of presidential elections set for 2028.

The case against Koroma dated to November 2023, when armed attackers stormed a military armoury, two barracks, two prisons and two police stations, clashing with security forces.

Twenty-one people were killed in what authorities deemed a coup attempt.

Two dozen soldiers and Koroma's former bodyguard were sentenced to prison terms ranging from 50 to 100 years by a military court for their alleged roles in the mutiny.

Koroma had briefly visited Sierra Leone in July, after the charges were dropped, during a summit of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) at the invitation of current President Julius Maada Bio.

items.title: Bentiu IDP camp court opens to strengthen access to justice
items.summary: BENTIU — A new court has opened at the Bentiu internally displaced persons’ camp in South Sudan’s Unity State as authorities seek to improve access to justice for displaced communities, according to the United Nations. The Bentiu IDP Camp Court supported by the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS), the Unity State government, the […] The post Bentiu IDP camp court opens to strengthen acc
items.body:
BENTIU — A new court has opened at the Bentiu internally displaced persons’ camp in South Sudan’s Unity State as authorities seek to improve access to justice for displaced communities, according to the United Nations.

The Bentiu IDP Camp Court supported by the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS), the Unity State government, the Judiciary of South Sudan, and the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs will operate from Sept. 7 to 26.

The court is expected to hear cases involving sexual and gender-based violence, drug-related offenses, and gang violence.

The Bentiu IDP Camp Court is an initiative of the Unity State Government’s Task Force on Combating Drug Abuse and Gang Violence, bringing together security, justice, and health actors.

The Court is being deployed in cooperation with the Community High Committee (CHC) of the Bentiu IDP Camp in response to repeated concerns and requests from the community for stronger justice and rule of law mechanisms to address drug use, gang violence, and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV), particularly affecting children and youth.

Its deployment aims to bring the formal justice system directly to residents of the IDP camp and provide an opportunity for serious offences to be investigated and adjudicated.

This deployment builds on the re-establishment of the Judiciary in Unity State in May 2026 after 13 years of absence and the seven mobile courts deployed across Unity State since 2024 to combat impunity, reduce violence, deter crime and contribute to peace and security in the State.

Bentiu IDP camp is South Sudan’s largest camp for internally displaced persons, hosting more than 100,000 people.

Established as a Protection of Civilians site following the outbreak of conflict in 2013, it was redesignated as an IDP camp in 2021 and remains a major focus of UNMISS’ civilian protection efforts in Bentiu.

Following the outbreak of conflict in 2013, permanent judicial and prosecutorial capacity was restored in Bentiu only in May 2026.

To support access to justice, combat impunity, and promote accountability in support of peace and security, UNMISS has supported the deployment of seven mobile courts across Unity State since 2024, including in Southern Unity and Mayom.

These courts have resulted in the adjudication of 517 cases, following a period in which no cases were adjudicated through the formal justice system in Unity State in 2023.

Sudans Post is an independent, young, and grass roots news media organization aimed at providing readers with an alternate depiction of events that occur on Sudan, South Sudan and East Africa, and to establish an engaging social platform for readers to discover and discuss the various issues that impact the two countries and the region.

items.title: Heavy Gunfire Sparks Fear of Renewed Fighting Near CAR’s Capital
items.summary: The renewed fighting reveals the fragile security situation in CAR, where peace agreements signed in recent years have repeatedly faltered, and where the government continues to struggle to assert authority beyond the capital. The post Heavy Gunfire Sparks Fear of Renewed Fighting Near CAR’s Capital appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: Intense fighting involving heavy and light weapons is taking place in the PK40-45 area along the Boali road, which leads to Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic (CAR). Traffic in and out of the capital via this road has been halted, preventing any vehicles from entering or leaving the town. Local sources in the CAR capital say they have yet to determine the forces involved in the ongoing chaos and exchange of fire. “At this stage, the exact circumstances leading to this exchange of gunfire are not known. No human and material casualty figures are available right now,” a government source who asked for anonymity because he is not authorised to speak on behalf of the government told HumAngle in Bangui. Diplomatic sources suggested that the exchange of gunfire happened between the CAR national army and some of the rebel groups operating in the country. There are currently no physical indications that the authorities in Bangui are preparing to send reinforcements to Boali. The heavy exchange of gunfire near the town of Boali comes amid an ongoing conflict in the country. When a coalition of rebel groups known as the Séléka overthrew President François Bozizé in 2013, CAR was thrown into a cycle of violence between different armed groups, government forces, and international peacekeepers. Despite the deployment of United Nations peacekeepers and bilateral support from allies such as Russia and Rwanda, a huge part of the country is still being controlled by armed rebel groups. The deadly groups often exploit CAR’s weak state institutions, porous borders, and lucrative natural resources, including diamonds and gold, to sustain their operations. The town of Boali strategically lies on the main road linking Bangui to the country’s northern and western regions. Vital for trade, supply routes, and military logistics, this corridor is contested by armed groups and state forces. Past clashes in this area have disrupted humanitarian access and heightened insecurity for civilians, many of whom already face displacement and food shortages. The renewed fighting reveals the fragile security situation in CAR, where peace agreements signed in recent years have repeatedly faltered, and where the government continues to struggle to assert authority beyond the capital. items.title: Amnesty International To Tinubu Govt: 37 Kaduna Worshippers Abducted During Easter Service Still In Captivity After Five Months
items.summary: Amnesty International To Tinubu Govt: 37 Kaduna Worshippers Abducted During Easter Service Still In Captivity After Five Months Amnesty International said the incident was one of several attacks demonstrating what it described as the “utter failure of Nigerian authorities to protect the people.”
items.body:
Amnesty International said the incident was one of several attacks demonstrating what it described as the “utter failure of Nigerian authorities to protect the people.”

Amnesty International has raised the alarm over the continued captivity of 37 worshippers abducted during raids on churches in Southern Kaduna, accusing the Nigerian government of failing to adequately protect citizens from recurring attacks, abductions and killings.

This comes despite assurances by President Bola Tinubu's administration that it is doing everything possible to protect citizens and secure the release of abductees.

The rights organisation on Monday, said the victims were abducted during Easter Sunday worship on April 5, 2026, in Ariko community, Kachia Local Government Area of Kaduna State, and have remained in captivity for five months.

Amnesty International said the incident was one of several attacks demonstrating what it described as the “utter failure of Nigerian authorities to protect the people.”

It said the prolonged captivity of the worshippers had been compounded by worsening conditions, with three of the 11 people abducted from Awon community reportedly dying in captivity within the week.

According to the organisation, a woman identified as Joy Samuel died on August 28 after giving birth in what it described as a deplorable condition. The baby she delivered also died.

It added that Mr. Yusuf Bawa, 34, and his five-year-old son also died in captivity as a result of severe illness and hunger.

“Three of the 11 people abducted from Awon community have died in captivity this week. A woman Joy Samuel died on 28 August, after giving birth in a deplorable condition. The baby she delivered also died. Mr. Yusuf Bawa 34, and his 5-year-old son have also died as a result of severe illness and hunger,” Amnesty International said.

The organisation said the deaths and illnesses suffered by the abducted persons reflected the harsh conditions and abuses they were allegedly being subjected to while in captivity.

“Deaths and severe illness these people are facing in captivity show the atrocities they are being subjected to,” it said.

Amnesty International further alleged that the victims were being subjected to repeated threats, starvation, sexual violence, beatings and other forms of degrading treatment.

“While in captivity, the abducted persons are always repeatedly threatened to be killed, starved, women and girls raped, beaten and dehumanized in so many ways,” the organisation said.

The rights group also expressed concern over the wider security situation in Southern Kaduna, saying recurring attacks, abductions for ransom and killings had continued to disrupt the lives of residents.

It said the insecurity had created a climate of fear that was affecting farming, education and other aspects of social life in communities across the region.

“Recurring attacks, abductions for ransom, and killings are continuing to make life a hell in many parts of southern Kaduna. A climate of fear is affecting agricultural activities, education and other aspects of social lives of the people,” Amnesty International said.

The organisation said the continued captivity of the worshippers underscored the need for the Nigerian government to intensify efforts to protect civilians and secure the release of people held by armed groups.

Amnesty International called on the government to fulfil its national and international human rights obligations by taking urgent steps to secure the safe release of the abducted worshippers.

“The Nigerian government must deliver on its national and international human rights obligations by immediately redoubling efforts to ensure the safe release and return of not only the 37 worshippers abducted in Kachia LGA, but also all people held captive by gunmen across Nigeria,” it said.

The organisation's concerns come as communities in Southern Kaduna continue to face security challenges, with attacks and abductions threatening livelihoods and access to education while leaving families of victims in prolonged uncertainty over the fate of their loved ones.

SaharaReporters reported in April that the Ariko community was plunged into mourning on Easter Sunday when suspected terrorists launched coordinated attacks on two churches, First ECWA Church and St. Augustine Catholic Church, killing at least seven worshippers and abducting several others.

Confirming the attack, the Councillor representing Awon Ward, Mark Bawa, said heavily armed assailants had stormed the area during early morning services.

items.title: Review: Historian Traces Boko Haram Back to Northern Nigeria’s Islamic History
items.summary: In a new book, academic historian Prof. Moses Ebe Ochonu argues that Boko Haram didn't invent its ideology from scratch but instead borrowed Dan Fodio’s 19th-century legacy to legitimise a different war with foreign inspiration. The post Review: Historian Traces Boko Haram Back to Northern Nigeria’s Islamic History appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: Boko Haram has been explained in over a dozen different ways in the past 17 years since it turned violent. Several factors – such as poverty, political exclusion, corruption, climate change, state violence, foreign jihadist influence, and failed governance – have been blamed. Each of these explanations gets at something real, but none of them quite answers why the movement took root in northeastern Nigeria specifically, how it justified its violence in Islamic terms, or why some audiences bought the message while most rejected it. In his recently released book, “ Boko Haram: The Past of the Present Upheaval ”, Moses Ebe Ochonu , a Nigerian professor of African History, looks into the issue long before Boko Haram waged its first attack. Instead of treating the insurgency as a modern phenomenon, Prof. Moses traces it through nearly two centuries of arguments over Islamic authority, reform, and political legitimacy in northern Nigeria. The cover page of Prof. Moses Ochonu’s book, “Boko Haram: The Past of the Present Upheaval”. In his words, “Boko Haram did not emerge in a historical vacuum. For this reason, the complex religious, political, and socioeconomic processes that birthed the movement should be examined within the long trajectory of Islamic reform and counterreform in Northern Nigeria.” (pp. 5–6) His recent work is among the more historically grounded studies of the insurgency. In putting together the book, he used Arabic texts, colonial archives, jihadist propaganda, and decades of Sokoto Caliphate scholarship to argue that Boko Haram sits inside a much longer line of reformist movements that have fought over what Islamic governance should look like in Northern Nigeria. The book does not claim a straight intellectual line runs from the 19th Sokoto jihad to Boko Haram. What it tries to show is how the militants kept invoking Usman dan Fodio’s memory to bolster their own claim to religious legitimacy. The real contribution of the book lies in showing that the fight over Boko Haram was never just a fight over territory or doctrine, but a fight over history’s legacy — a struggle to claim that what the Sokoto jihad left behind is what Boko Haram is trying to restore. History as a weapon Prof. Moses’ argument rests on the premise that Dan Fodio occupies an important position in the region’s religious imagination, with almost every sect seeking to associate itself with him. Dan Fodio not only founded the Sokoto Caliphate; his descendants include the current Sultan of Sokoto, and his writings still carry weight in Islamic scholarship across West Africa. The book shows how both the founder of Boko Haram , Mohammed Yusuf, and its most violent leader, Abubakar Shekau , leaned on Dan Fodio’s name in their sermons and propaganda, framing colonialism and the modern Nigerian state as a break from an earlier Islamic order founded by Dan Fodio and which their movement claimed to be restoring. Their attempt to tie Boko Haram to the Sokoto jihad was deliberately designed to give them a way to fit a new insurgency into a story northern Nigerians already knew. A screenshot from one video in which Mohammed Yusuf was delivering a sermon and clips of other Boko Haram-related incidents. To expose that, the book quotes Mohammed Yusuf in one of his speeches, claiming that during Dan Fodio’s time “it was the Shari’a that was the practice in this country. Dan Fodio and other Islamic scholars carried out the jihad and ensured that Qur’anic law was implemented. Allah did not interfere with this situation until when our Muslim leaders accepted… the Europeans’ secular constitution.” (p. 3) However, Mohammed’s argument relies on a selective and fundamentally dishonest reading of history. Prof. Moses exposes the Boko Haram leader’s historical reference as a performance rather than a genuine doctrinal inheritance. Furthermore, the book distinguishes historical continuity from theological continuity because they are not the same thing. A clear line is shown between political symbolism and doctrinal influence. Boko Haram claimed Dan Fodio’s legacy, but it grew out of a different intellectual world, with roots in 20th-century Salafi reformism , global jihadist literature, and arguments that did not yet exist in Dan Fodio’s time. Theologically, Dan Fodio worked within the Sufi spiritualism – a tradition within Islam that emphasises inner devotion and spiritual purification, Ash’ari theology – a Sunni sect that uses rationalism alongside scriptures, and Maliki jurisprudence – one of the four Sunni schools of Islamic law – dominated West African Islam during his life. Boko Haram, by constrast, belongs to the Salafi-jihadi current – an extremist ideology that combines Salafi interpretation of Islam with an emphasis of Jihad as a primary purpose of the religion, which draws on ideas from well beyond northern Nigeria and is ideologically at odds with much of what Dan Fodio stood for. Prof. Moses doesn’t reduce the movement to foreign influence, though. His argument is that Boko Haram picked and chose while combining global jihadist ideas with regional symbols that would resonate locally. That keeps the book from falling into either trap of treating Boko Haram as either purely homegrown or purely imported. “The claim here is not that there is a direct instructional value in this preexisting jihad template for Boko Haram; rather, the point is to highlight the fact that Boko Haram… see[s] [itself] as continuing in the Dan Fodio jihad tradition… This history and tradition of reform, dissidence, and jihad have collectively become an all-purpose alibi to draw on.” (p. 23) From reform to radicalisation The book covers how Islamic reform movements changed in postcolonial northern Nigeria, tracing how a reformist current hardened into one that insurgents could later claim as their own. The author devotes considerable attention to the intellectual and spiritual founder of Jama’atu Izalatil Bidi’a Wa Iqamatus Sunnah (Izala), Sheikh Mahmud Gumi, and to the reformist currents that pushed back against established Sufi institutions in the latter half of the 20th century. Gumi’s movement reshaped religious debate across northern Nigeria and introduced new forms of scriptural literalism that influenced later generations. “Gumi was instrumental to the long process of Islamic dissidence that transformed the Northern Nigerian Muslim landscape from a predominantly Sufi one to one that came to be suffused in anti-Sufi [ideas].” (pp. 95-96) Even so, one notices that the author is careful not to draw a straight line from reform to violence. Reformist Salafism did not cause extremism, but he argues it changed the religious landscape enough that more radical figures later found room to claim authority within it. He notes that many scholars associated with reformist Salafism rejected armed rebellion outright, yet the intellectual climate they helped create still left an opening that more militant voices eventually filled. “The theological creeds of the Salafi clerics and the religious activists who embraced political Islam did not emerge from a historical void… While the analysis of this historical tapestry is not intended to be read as a linear progression, I argue that the ideational transformations resulting from successive reformist projects made the Boko Haram moment, if not Boko Haram itself, possible.” (p. 10) Abubakar Shekau. The book also examines how Boko Haram justified violence. Prof. Moses places the insurgency’s arguments inside long-running debates over governance, apostasy, religious reform, and what Muslim rulers owe their subjects. Readers may reject the movement’s conclusions, but the book insists its ideology can be still be understood rather than dismissed without examination. That framing, according to the author, also explains why Boko Haram kept reaching for local historical references even while aligning itself with global Salafi-jihadist networks. Groups tied to al-Qaeda or the Islamic State bring transnational frameworks with them, but they still need local stories to establish credibility in the places where they actually operate. In northern Nigeria, the memory of the Sokoto Caliphate became that story for Boko Haram. On ISWAP The closing chapters briefly turn to the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP). Prof. Moses draws a line between ISWAP and Jama’atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda’awati Wal-Jihad (JAS) —Boko Haram’s formal name. Rather than leaning mainly on indiscriminate violence, ISWAP has put more effort into building administrative structures, collecting taxes, and cultivating ties with the civilians under its influence. “The former [ISWAP] predicated its decision to split from the latter [Shekau’s JAS] on Shekau’s flagrant flouting of jihad rules, which it interpreted as a debasement of the jihad ideal. The distinction between the tactics of Boko Haram’s two factions is significant and has become the major touchstone of the ongoing scorched-earth clashes betwe

items.title: UN envoy presses Sudan leader on truce and prisoner exchange
items.summary: The UN special envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto, has urged de-escalation of hostilities, and the... The post UN envoy presses Sudan leader on truce and prisoner exchange appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .
items.body: The UN special envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto, has urged de-escalation of hostilities, and the protection of civilians in talks with Sudan’s army chief and Sovereignty Council chair, Gen Abdelfattah El Burhan, while raising the prospect of exchanging prisoners and civilian detainees. Haavisto held a series of meetings in Khartoum on Sunday with Burhan, who heads the Sovereign Council and the army, Prime Minister Kamil Idris, Finance Minister and Justice and Equality Movement (JEM) leader Jibril Ibrahim, focusing on developments in the country, reducing tensions, ongoing consultations on dialogue, and ways to end the war and achieve peace in Sudan. In a statement after meeting El Burhan, Haavisto says dialogue is the path to sustainable peace and a comprehensive ceasefire. He says he is ready to cooperate and engage closely with all Sudanese parties and stakeholders, and to work with partners in the Quintet to advance the political process, ensuring that it is inclusive, integrated, and responsive to the aspirations of the Sudanese people. Haavisto says he conveyed important messages to El Burhan concerning de-escalation and the protection of civilians. “I look forward to continuing our meetings towards an exchange of prisoners and civilian detainees, in close cooperation with the International Committee of the Red Cross,” he says. Kamil Idris during his meeting with Pekka Haavisto in Khartoum on Sunday, September 6, 2026 (Soverignty Council Media) Sovereignty first Prime Minister Kamil Idris told the UN envoy that Sudan’s leadership will not compromise on national sovereignty or sovereign decision-making, stressing the country’s complete rejection of all forms of foreign intervention. Jibril Ibrahim told the envoy that the Sudanese Armed Forces are the national institution constitutionally responsible for protecting the country and defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity. JEM rejects wider arms embargo Ibrahim says the Justice and Equality Movement (JEM) rejects proposals to expand the arms embargo currently imposed on Darfur to cover the whole of Sudan. Such a measure, he says, would conflict with national sovereignty and restrict the armed forces’ ability to carry out their constitutional duty of protecting the country. He calls on the United Nations to welcome and support the Sudanese dialogue initiative, and to work with Sudanese parties to develop it into an inclusive, Sudanese-owned political process capable of ending the war and laying the foundations for lasting peace and a stable state. Dr. Jibril Ibrahim, head of the Justice and Equality Movement and Minister of Finance, during his meeting with UN envoy Pekka Haavisto on Sunday, September 6, 2026 (Photo: Supplied) Note: This report has been translated from Arabic with the assistance of artificial intelligence tools, and subsequently reviewed and adapted by a human editor before publication. Share article The post UN envoy presses Sudan leader on truce and prisoner exchange appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .

items.title: Libya arrests five people in connection with drone strikes on refinery
items.summary: Authorities in western Libya have arrested five people including foreigners who were involved in a recent string of drone attacks on a major energy complex, the Tripoli-based government said on Sunday.
items.body:
Authorities in western Libya have arrested five people in connection with a recent string of drone attacks on a major energy facility.

The government said the arrests exposed a “vast plot” and described the attacks as part of a coordinated campaign.

Authorities said the group were part of a "sabotage cell" who also planned to attack a power station south of Tripoli, as well as other vital facilities.

They said foreigners are among the suspects but didn’t give further details.

In August, a large petrol reservoir in Zawiya caught fire during a drone attack on a major oil facility near Tripoli, Libya's state-owned oil company NOC said.

The reservoir is part of the second-largest oil refinery in Libya, with a refining capacity of 120,000 barrels per day. Other drone attacks followed at the Zawiya complex, which is located some 45 kilometres west of Tripoli.

On Thursday, another attack on fuel tanks outside of Tripoli was thwarted, the NOC said.

Libya has the largest oil reserves in Africa. But the country has been beset by violence and instability since the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

Two governments are currently vying for power: the UN-recognised administration in Tripoli led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, and a rival in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.

items.title: Somali cleric Ali Wajis endorses killing of government critics
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A prominent pro-government religious scholar told a gathering of senior Somali officials, including the defense minister, on Sunday that people who oppose the administration of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud should be treated as terrorists and killed – a statement that has alarmed opposition figures already on edge after a drone strike wounded […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A prominent pro-government religious scholar told a gathering of senior Somali officials, including the defense minister, on Sunday that people who oppose the administration of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud should be treated as terrorists and killed – a statement that has alarmed opposition figures already on edge after a drone strike wounded a former security chief turned government critic on Thursday. Sheikh Ali Wajis, a cleric known for his consistent public backing of the Federal Government, made the remarks at a meeting attended by government officials, including the Minister of Defense. “Anyone who fights Somalia’s current government should face the same punishment as terrorists and should be killed,” Wajis told the gathering. Neither Wajis nor the Ministry of Defense could be reached for comment. Villa Somalia had not issued a statement responding to the remarks as of publication, and no official who attended Sunday’s meeting has publicly distanced the government from them. Coming on the heels of an attack on an opposition figure Wajis’s remarks land just days after a strike on the residence of Gen. Mahad Abdirahman Aden , widely known as “Taliye Shub,” in the border town of Doolow, in the Gedo region. Gen. Mahad, Somalia’s former Custodial Corps commander, was wounded in the attack along with his wife and several others; at least one person, reported to be an Ethiopian domestic worker, was killed. He was evacuated for treatment across the border in Ethiopia. Gen. Mahad, who was removed from his post earlier this year and briefly placed under house arrest, has since emerged as a vocal critic of the Federal Government and is aligned with the political camp of former Southwest State President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Laftagareen.” Authorities in Jubaland have accused Turkish military aircraft of carrying out the strike, calling it a deliberate, politically motivated attack tied to Gen. Mahad’s opposition to Mogadishu. In a statement, Jubaland said two missiles were fired, with one also striking the residence of Doolow’s district commissioner. The Federal Government has denied any involvement in an airstrike, offering a different account of what caused the damage to the house. Turkey, which has become one of Somalia’s most significant military partners, providing training, equipment and air support, has not publicly responded to the accusation. The disputed strike triggered protests in Doolow, with residents demanding an independent investigation into who was responsible and why Gen. Mahad’s residence was targeted. A cleric with a history of hardline rhetoric This is not the first time Wajis, who has served as an adviser to successive Somali administrations, has taken a hardline public stance in defense of the government. In April, as Somali National Army desertions mounted during Al-Shabab’s offensive in the Shabelle regions, Wajis publicly branded soldiers who fled their posts as apostates and called for their arrest – remarks that were echoed at the time by a senior Custodial Corps commander, who warned that deserters and their families could face arrest or execution. His latest comments arrive at a moment of unusually sharp strain between Mogadishu and Somalia’s federal member states. Jubaland, Puntland and ousted Southwest administration have all rejected constitutional amendments extending federal institutions’ mandates, and have formally suspended ties with the Federal Government, accusing it of interference in their political and security affairs. Why it matters Coming so soon after an unresolved and contested attack on a prominent opposition-aligned general, a call from a cleric closely associated with the presidency – delivered in front of the defense minister – for opponents of the government to be killed is likely to deepen fears among opposition figures and federal member states that political dissent in Somalia is being conflated with terrorism. Independent verification of the strike’s origin, and any government response to Wajis’s remarks, remained pending as of publication. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com
