items.title: 22 killed in wedding venue fire in DR Congo: Mayor
items.summary: Investigation launched to determine cause of deadly blaze, mayor says
items.body:
At least 22 people were killed and several others injured when a fire broke out at a wedding venue in the Democratic Republic of Congo's capital Kinshasa on Saturday, a local official said.

The fire erupted during a wedding reception at a building in Kinshasa's Lingwala commune, according to Lingwala Mayor Norbert Mushinga.

"After inspecting the place, I can confirm that the provisional death toll stands at 22," Mushinga told reporters in Kinshasa.

"People faced difficulties reaching the emergency exit; everyone was in a state of panic," he said.

Mushinga said property inside the building was also destroyed and several injured people were taken to health facilities in Kinshasa for treatment.

He said an investigation has been launched to ascertain the cause of the fire, with an electrical fault suspected.

In a statement, Interior Minister Jacquemain Shabani directed all provincial governors to conduct immediate inspections of venues hosting public events.

Shabani ordered authorities to close any establishments that do not meet safety standards.

items.title: Somalia: Fahad Yasin links Jama to Gen. Shub drone strike
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s former intelligence chief Fahad Yasin has accused the Speaker of the House of the People, Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur – widely known by the nicknames “Jama” and “Minister TikTok” – of directing the drone strike that hit the Doolow residence of former Custodial Corps commander Gen. Mahad Abdirahman Aden late Thursday. Gen. […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s former intelligence chief Fahad Yasin has accused the Speaker of the House of the People, Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur – widely known by the nicknames “Jama” and “Minister TikTok” – of directing the drone strike that hit the Doolow residence of former Custodial Corps commander Gen. Mahad Abdirahman Aden late Thursday. Gen. Mahad, popularly known as “General Shub,” survived the overnight attack in the Gedo region town near the Ethiopian border. Jubaland’s Ministry of Information, Culture and Tourism said five people in total were hurt: Gen. Mahad, who sustained minor injuries, and four civilians, including his wife. The allegation In a Facebook statement, Yasin warned that the strike would carry “dangerous repercussions capable of spreading beyond Somalia to neighboring countries,” a remark he made in the context of accusing President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s administration of crossing a dangerous line. Yasin said Nur first demonstrated what he described as command responsibility for lethal operations in December 2017, when he served as acting head of the National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) and, according to Yasin, led the raid on the Mogadishu home of opposition politician Abdirahman Abdishakur Warsame. Yasin alleged that Nur – who is now serving as acting president while President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud is on an overseas trip – has again used that authority, this time to direct the strike on Gen. Mahad. Competing accounts of the attack Jubaland’s Ministry of Information, Culture and Tourism said Turkish military aircraft carried out the overnight operation, adding that two missiles were fired – one of which struck the home of Doolow’s district chairman. Other Jubaland officials and prominent political figures, including former presidents Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and Mohamed Abdullahi Farmaajo and the opposition Somali Future Council, have echoed the drone-strike account and demanded an independent investigation. The Federal Government has denied involvement and disputed that a drone strike took place at all. Its preliminary investigation, officials said, indicates the blast at Gen. Mahad’s residence originated from explosives being handled inside the house rather than from an external strike. Turkey, which operates a military base in Mogadishu and trains and equips federal government forces, has not responded to the allegations that its aircraft were involved. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com

items.title: Niger blames France for inciting failed mutiny, Paris denies involvement
items.summary: Niger has blamed France for inciting last week’s failed military mutiny, according ‌to a government statement read on television on Friday. Paris has denied any involvement in the attack.
items.body:
Niger has blamed France for inciting last week’s thwarted military mutiny , according ‌to a government statement read on television on Friday and cited by Reuters and AFP.

On August 29, disgruntled soldiers attacked a strategic army base in Niamey and fired shots near the presidential palace. But the army and its Russian paramilitary allies eventually neutralised the mutiny .

The unrest killed three members of the presidential guard, according to Niger's Foreign Affairs Ministry. AFP reported a total number of five deaths, including civilians.

On Friday, Niger’s Council of Ministers said it had concluded that the attack had been incited by ‌a ⁠vast network of accomplices led by France, Niger's former colonial power.

"A substantial body of evidence has been compiled regarding this attack, and Niger ​reserves the ​right to ⁠bring the matter before international courts," the government said in the ​statement quoted by Reuters

In response, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot denied any involvement of France in the attack.

"These are nothing but pure fantasies," Barrot told French radio station RFI on Saturday. "All of this is, as usual, a way of wrongly blaming France for something it is simply not responsible for."

According to RFI, on Tuesday already, a Nigerian military official had appeared on television to accuse several states, including France, Ivory Coast and Benin, of supporting the mutiny.

Like its fellow junta-run Sahel neighbours in Burkina Faso and Mali, Niger has turned its back on Paris since the 2023 coup that brought General Abdourahamane Tiani to power.

All three have sought closer ties with Russia in tackling the region's deadly jihadist conflict, which has continued to rage unabated.

items.title: Ethiopia questions Somali soldiers who crossed border to visit families in Somalia
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Ethiopia’s security agencies have begun interrogating dozens of Somali National Army (SNA) soldiers who crossed into Ethiopian territory after completing training in Somalia’s Galmudug region, according to reports by regional media. Around 80 soldiers crossed into Ethiopia’s Somali region following the training, which was funded by Saudi Arabia and saw roughly 3,000 […
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Ethiopia’s security agencies have begun interrogating dozens of Somali National Army (SNA) soldiers who crossed into Ethiopian territory after completing training in Somalia’s Galmudug region, according to reports by regional media. Around 80 soldiers crossed into Ethiopia’s Somali region following the training, which was funded by Saudi Arabia and saw roughly 3,000 SNA members graduate at once. The soldiers have since been taken to Jigjiga, the capital of Ethiopia’s Somali region. Most of the soldiers are reported to have come from Somalia’s Bakol region and were on their way to their original homes at the time. The soldiers were reportedly on authorized leave, as confirmed by Somalia’s National Security Advisor Aways Hajji Yusuf, and had chosen to take a long detour through Ethiopian territory for security reasons, in order to avoid possible attacks by Al-Shabaab. The militant group controls major roads connecting Somalia’s Hiran and Bakol regions along the border with Ethiopia. The soldiers were recruited from El Barde in Bakol region and nearby villages, and mostly belong to the Ogaden clan. Latest reports indicate that both Ethiopia’s Somali region and the federal government in Addis Ababa were fully aware of the arrangement. It is not clear, however, why the soldiers have been taken to Jigjiga for interrogation. There has been no announcement from Ethiopia, the Somali region, or the Somali federal government about the current location of the troops or the wider circumstances surrounding the case. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com

items.title: Guinea buries 36 victims of Conakry landfill collapse
items.summary: Thousands of people attended a mass funeral held in Guinea on Friday for the 36 people killed in a landfill collapse in a suburb of the capital last month.
items.body:
Guinea held a mass funeral attended by thousands on Friday for the 36 people killed in a landfill collapse in a suburb of the capital last month following heavy rains.

Many of the victims were sleeping when part of the massive garbage dump, located near homes in the Dar-es-Salam neighbourhood, gave way overnight between August 22 and 23.

During the ceremony Friday, authorities announced an updated toll of 36, including that there were 17 Sierra Leonean nationals among the dead.

The three dozen bodies were taken to a mosque in Bambeto, a Conakry suburb, for Muslim funeral prayers.

Many mourners struggled to make sense of the tragedy . "We are completely disillusioned. We are deeply troubled by this tragedy. We don’t know what to do," said Aboubacar Camara, who survived the collapse.

Among the crowd of thousands, several women overcome with grief fell into a trance-like state, an AFP journalist witnessed.

"Guinea is in mourning, and we share the suffering of the victims' loved ones," Conakry Governor General Mahawa Cisse said during the ceremony.

Afterwards, the bodies were taken to the Bambeto cemetery for their burial, attended by family, religious leaders and government officials.

Around twenty people remain hospitalised, and more than 1,600 people have received assistance, according to the country's emergency management agency.

Since the collapse, authorities have been demolishing houses in the zone considered at risk from the rubbish dump, citing the need to protect the population from another tragedy.

The residents have criticised the difficult conditions under which the operation was carried out and are calling for relocation assistance.

items.title: EXPLAINER - From Ethiopia border to Darfur: Where are Sudan’s war fronts heating up?
items.summary: Blue Nile, Kordofan, Darfur emerge as key theaters as army, RSF, allied forces battle for strategic towns, supply routes, border areas
items.body:
Sudan’s most active battlefronts stretch across a vast arc from the Blue Nile state near the Ethiopian border in the east, through three Kordofan states, to Darfur in the west.

Al-Baraka, Bakori, Geissan and Kurmuk in the Blue Nile; Bara, Al-Abbasiya and Kauda in Kordofan; and Um Baru, Kernoi and Abu Suruj in Darfur have emerged as some of the most significant centers of fighting and military movement.

Control of the areas is divided among the army, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and armed groups allied with each side. Drone attacks have increasingly carried the war into towns and villages far from traditional front lines.

Anadolu reviewed the main hotspots, their military significance and the current balance of control.

Al-Baraka, in the Kurmuk locality in the southeastern Blue Nile state, has become one of the newest fronts between the army on one side and the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), on the other.

The area lies on the outskirts of Kurmuk near the Ethiopian border, giving it strategic importance for movements between border zones and the interior of Blue Nile.

On Friday, the army said it repelled an attack by the RSF and SPLM-N on Al-Baraka.

The army’s 4th Infantry Division said forces inflicted personnel and equipment losses on the attackers and forced them to retreat toward the Sudan-Ethiopia border.

Bakori, in the Geissan locality, is another key hotspot in Blue Nile.

The area hosts a military base and the headquarters of the army’s 14th Brigade, making it a contested position for both sides.

Bakori lies 170 kilometers (106 miles) southeast of Damazin, the state capital.

In recent weeks, the RSF and SPLM-N have taken control of Geissan and Kurmuk, the administrative centers of the two localities bearing the same names.

The army, however, continues to hold other parts of both localities, as well as Damazin, Er Roseires and the localities of Bau, Wad al-Mahi and Tadamon.

Beyond Kurmuk and Geissan, the SPLM-N, led by Abdelaziz al-Hilu, has controlled Yabus since 2011.

The area, one of the movement’s main strongholds in Blue Nile, lies near the borders with Ethiopia and South Sudan, around 80 kilometers from Kurmuk.

The SPLM-N has fought the Sudanese government since 2011, demanding greater autonomy in Blue Nile and South Kordofan before joining forces with the RSF during the current war.

In North Kordofan, Bara remains one of the most strategically important towns because of its location on the national highway linking it to Omdurman, west of the national capital, Khartoum.

In late July, the army retook Bara, Jabra al-Sheikh and Um Sayala, allowing it to secure the highway and reshape the military balance in the state bordering Darfur and West Kordofan.

Fighting around Bara has since shifted largely from direct ground clashes to drone attacks on military positions and villages surrounding the town.

Villages west of Bara that contain no military deployments have also come under RSF attacks, according to the Emergency Lawyers and the Sudan Doctors Network.

Other military movements are concentrated in northwestern North Kordofan, where the RSF controls Hamrat al-Sheikh, Al-Mazroub and Sodari.

Their importance stems from their proximity to Darfur and West Kordofan, and their location along movement and supply routes connecting the two regions.

North Kordofan has also faced repeated drone attacks, alongside similar strikes in South and West Kordofan.

In South Kordofan, Kadugli and Dilling remain among the most important army-held positions.

The army broke the siege on both cities months ago, and strengthened its control in large parts of the state, except for areas still held by the SPLM-N under al-Hilu.

Although major ground fighting around the two cities has subsided, both continue to face intermittent drone attacks that have killed and wounded civilians.

The Al-Abbasiya locality has become another hotspot in South Kordofan amid repeated attacks and deteriorating security conditions.

On Thursday, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said 6,420 people had been displaced from nine villages in Al-Abbasiya because of worsening insecurity from Sept. 1 to 2.

Kauda, in the far south of South Kordofan, remains under SPLM-N control and is one of the movement’s most important strongholds.

Alongside its role in the broader conflict between the SPLM-N and the government, Kauda has also witnessed local fighting between SPLM-N forces and members of the Otoro tribe because of a land dispute.

The clashes began in late June after a dispute about border demarcation between the Shawaya and Otoro tribes escalated into armed conflict, killing dozens and displacing thousands.

North Darfur remains one of the most active fronts in the Darfur region, with the army and the Joint Force of Armed Movements conducting operations against the RSF.

The Joint Force includes armed groups such as the Sudan Liberation Movement, led by Minni Arko Minnawi, and the Justice and Equality Movement, led by Jibril Ibrahim.

Um Baru and Karnoi have emerged as key hotspots after the army and Joint Force gained control of large parts of both localities.

Their proximity to the Chadian border makes them important bases for advancing into other parts of North Darfur and securing supply routes in the state.

In West Darfur, army and Joint Force movements have been concentrated north of El Geneina, the state capital.

In June, the forces captured Kulbus, about 160 kilometers north of El Geneina, before withdrawing more than two weeks later and repositioning around the town.

The army and the Joint Force later took Bir Saliba and Jebel Moon north of El Geneina as part of efforts to expand their foothold in the state.

On Aug. 29, West Darfur Gov. Bahr al-Din Adam Karama said the army and the Joint Force had taken control of Abu Suruj in the Sirba locality following clashes with the RSF.

Abu Suruj is among the latest areas where territorial control has shifted in West Darfur as military movements continue north of El Geneina.

The RSF and allied forces still control most of Darfur, while the army and the Joint Force maintain positions in parts of the region’s north and west.

Despite the different strategic value of each front, displacement remains the most consistent consequence of the widening conflict.

In Blue Nile, the IOM said 3,000 people had been displaced from three villages in the Kurmuk locality, while the UN estimated that 22,000 people fled fighting in Geissan in one week.

In South Kordofan, 6,420 people were displaced from villages in Al-Abbasiya, in addition to thousands forced from their homes by the conflict in Kauda.

The growing use of drones has also expanded the threat well beyond frontline areas. The UN said 1,100 civilians were killed in drone attacks between January and June.

The army and RSF have been at war since April 2023 because of disputes surrounding the political transition and plans to integrate the paramilitary force into the regular military.

As front lines continue to shift between Blue Nile, Kordofan and Darfur, Sudan’s map of military hotspots remains fluid, with no clear prospect of an end to the war.

items.title: SPLA-IO spokesman rules out armed infighting despite leadership crisis
items.summary: JUBA – South Sudan’s main armed opposition group will not descend into armed infighting despite a deepening leadership crisis that has split senior officials over who should run the movement in the absence of detained leader Riek Machar, its military spokesman said on Friday. Speaking to Sudans Post in an interview on Friday, SPLA-IO spokesman […] The post SPLA-IO spokesman rules out armed infight
items.body:
SPLA-IO deputy spokesman Col. Lam Paul Gabriel speaks to media about the progress and challenges facing the transitional security arrangement in Juba on October 2, 2019. [Photo by Getty Images] JUBA – South Sudan’s main armed opposition group will not descend into armed infighting despite a deepening leadership crisis that has split senior officials over who should run the movement in the absence of detained leader Riek Machar, its military spokesman said on Friday.

Speaking to Sudans Post in an interview on Friday, SPLA-IO spokesman Col. Lam Paul Gabriel described the dispute as primarily an administrative and constitutional disagreement, ruling out the possibility that it would lead to armed clashes between forces aligned with the rival leadership camps.

“What is currently happening is administrative issues, understanding the constitution of the movement and how it’s supposed to function,” Lam said.

“It is not really something that will trigger violence, as people might think, that maybe there will be clashes between the SPLA-IO forces. That is not going to happen because the SPLA-IO is bigger than an individual or a few individuals.”

The comments follow days of turmoil within the SPLM/A-IO after Oyet Nathaniel Pierino, Machar’s deputy who had been serving as acting chairman and commander-in-chief, suspended interim Secretary-General Regina Joseph Kaba and seven other senior officials on August 31.

Oyet accused the officials of trying to undermine his authority, establish parallel structures and separate the movement’s political and military wings. He described their actions as a “conspiracy and coup attempt” and said his measures were intended to prevent the SPLM-IO from collapsing and disintegrating.

Kaba and other Political Bureau members rejected Oyet’s move and issued a counter-order suspending him , accusing him of defying collective leadership and taking unilateral decisions that had contributed to deaths and divisions within the movement.

Lam said the SPLA-IO military command had endorsed the Political Bureau’s decision and no longer regarded Oyet as the movement’s acting leader.

“Honorable Oyet Nathaniel is not currently the acting chair of the SPLM-IO, but he is just a member,” Lam said. “He will wait for that to be revoked or for him to be reinstated. I don’t know when, but that is something that can only happen when there is another sitting probably done and when there is an investigation as to why he got suspended.”

He said Kaba was now in charge of the political wing while Lt. Gen. Peter Thok headed the military as acting chief of general staff, with communication between the political leadership and forces expected to pass through the military chain of command.

Senior SPLA-IO commanders meeting this week adopted the Political Bureau resolutions, recognized Kaba as Acting Interim Deputy Chair and reaffirmed Thok as the only Acting Chief of General Staff, according to a statement issued by Lam.

Lam also said Machar had previously instructed Oyet to halt military deployments and political assignments after some of the changes allegedly contributed to deaths in Nasir and Panyijiar.

“Due to that, we were able to receive a message from our chair and commander-in-chief, which was sent also to Honorable Nathaniel to stop all these deployments for now to avoid the death of these innocent civilians or some soldiers who might have taken matters into their hands,” Lam said.

He said the communication also made clear that responsibility for the army rested with Thok and that instructions to SPLA-IO forces should pass through the acting chief of general staff.

Lam, however, stopped short of saying that Machar had personally approved the Political Bureau’s latest decision to suspend Oyet.

“One thing I’ll be very sincere with you is that when it comes to the status of Dr. Riek currently, I can’t tell whether he is communicating or is not communicating,” he said.

Lam said he nevertheless believed Machar was aware of the developments, arguing that information could reach him despite his detention.

“I can’t rule out completely that he did not get this information,” Lam said. “I know he got and I believe he got this information that Honorable Regina is now the acting interim deputy chair of the SPLM/SPLA.”

Lam provided no evidence that Machar had received the Political Bureau resolution, and his remarks reflected his belief rather than confirmation of direct communication with the detained opposition leader.

Machar has been detained in Juba since March 2025 following a political and security crisis triggered by fighting in Nasir. His prolonged absence has left the movement grappling with questions over how far officials acting on his behalf can exercise his political and military powers.

The SPLM-IO’s official website continued to list Machar as chairman and commander-in-chief and Oyet as deputy chairman this week, though the site may not yet reflect the latest internal decisions.

Asked about statements from some commanders and structures continuing to recognize Oyet, Lam said individual officers could support him personally but insisted that such declarations did not represent the SPLA-IO as an institution.

“The army, the SPLM/SPLA or the SPLA, does not belong to an individual. Let’s just put this clear and everybody should understand this,” he said. “It belongs to the system. It belongs to this movement.”

Lam acknowledged that Oyet retained support among some soldiers, which he linked partly to Oyet’s continued public campaign for Machar’s release.

“If Honorable Oyet moves aside just a little bit and says, ‘I don’t understand the document,’ you will see how many people will say no to him,” Lam said.

“But it is because he still says that, ‘I am still fighting for the release of Dr. Machar.’ Some soldiers still have got that respect for him for that. And that’s why they are standing with him.”

He said declarations of support for Oyet by individual military figures should not be confused with the official position of the army.

“If there are individuals within the army that want to say that they stand with Nathaniel, these are individuals, but not the SPLM-IO,” he said.

Lam rejected suggestions that the current turmoil demonstrated that Machar had failed to prepare the movement to survive his absence.

He said SPLA-IO soldiers remained loyal to Machar and argued that the movement had not prepared for such a situation because Machar had instead sought to unify opposition and government forces under the 2018 peace agreement.

“These soldiers are loyal to Dr. Machar. That’s why up to today, they are dying. They are fighting, they are defending themselves, they are defending the people under their control because of Dr. Machar,” Lam said.

He said Machar’s intention upon returning to Juba was not to preserve the SPLA-IO indefinitely as a separate force, but to have the rival armies unified into a national military under the peace deal.

“That was why we never prepared for this situation,” Lam said. “So it’s not the fault of Dr. Machar. It is just because he loved peace and he wanted change in this country.”

Lam acknowledged, however, that there was bitterness among SPLA-IO soldiers over the decision to return to Juba and place their faith in the peace process.

“People, in fact, including myself, I’m bitter. I’m bitter just like almost every soldier who is bitter in the bush, questioning why did we go to Juba and prepare because people didn’t trust the regime. They know the regime was going to cause problems,” he said.

Despite the bitterness within the ranks and the competing claims to leadership, Lam insisted the dispute would remain political and administrative and would not lead to armed infighting within the SPLA-IO.

items.title: Sudan doctors group says 21 killed in RSF-allied SPLM-N attack in South Kordofan
items.summary: Sudan Doctors Network says women, children among victims, accuses group of targeting civilians on an ‘ethnic basis’
items.body:
At least 21 people, including women and children, were killed in an attack by the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), allied with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in South Kordofan state, the Sudan Doctors Network said on Friday.

The independent medical network said in a statement that the attack targeted the Debi and Luweiri areas, south and west of Kauda, which are inhabited by the Atoro tribe.

The SPLM-N forces attacked areas in South Kordofan, killing the victims including women and children, and injuring others, the network said, adding the attack attack also forced a large number of civilians to flee the area.

It condemned the attack and accused SPLM-N forces of targeting civilians “on an ethnic basis” and displacing large numbers of them from their areas.

The Sudan Doctors Network described the attack as “a blatant violation of international humanitarian law and the rules protecting civilians.”

On Aug. 25, the Sudan Doctors Network said 27 people, including four children, were killed in attacks it accused the SPLM-N of carrying out on two areas in South Kordofan “on an ethnic basis.”

On Aug. 20, SPLM-N forces took control of Kauda, the group’s stronghold, as part of a wider military operation to suppress an Atoro tribe rebellion in areas of Heiban locality in South Kordofan.

On July 2, the Sudanese government condemned the “bloody events and grave violations” in Kauda, saying they left civilians dead and injured.

The clashes followed fighting between the SPLM-N and a group from the Atoro tribe after disputes about border demarcation between the Shawaya and Atoro tribes turned into armed confrontations.

On May 13, the Sudan Doctors Network said more than 61 people were killed, including nine children and five women, in clashes between the SPLM-N and a group from the Atoro tribe in Kauda.

The Al-Hilu-led SPLM-N has fought the Sudanese government since 2011, demanding autonomy in South Kordofan and Blue Nile regions.

Since April 2023, the Sudanese army and the RSF have been locked in a war that erupted because of disputes regarding the integration of the paramilitary force into the military.

The war has killed tens of thousands and displaced around 13 million, while creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian and hunger crises.

items.title: Turkey accused of war crime after drone strike on former Somali commander
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A drone strike tore through the residence of General Mahad Abdirahman, Somalia’s former custodial corps chief, in the border town of Dolow on Thursday, and he survived it – but the attack has ignited a political firestorm, with Jubaland authorities pointing at Turkey and warning that a dangerous new front has opened […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A drone strike tore through the residence of General Mahad Abdirahman, Somalia’s former custodial corps chief, in the border town of Dolow on Thursday, and he survived it – but the attack has ignited a political firestorm, with Jubaland authorities pointing at Turkey and warning that a dangerous new front has opened in Somalia’s fracturing security landscape. A video circulating online showed the general receiving treatment at a hospital in the Ethiopian side of Dolow, the twin town separated from its Somali counterpart by the border. A retaliatory strike, hours after Baidoa attack The strike came only hours after Darwish forces loyal to ousted Southwest State President Abdiasis Laftagaren stormed the city of Baidoa on Thursday morning, overrunning army bases and briefly seizing parts of the city’s neighborhoods before fierce clashes. General Mahad is reported to be the backbone of Laftagaren’s resistance against the federal government, which seized Baidoa in a late-March offensive backed from the air by the Turkish air force. He is also Laftagaren’s father-in-law and a prominent figure commanding wide support among the population of Baidoa. The drone strike on his home is reported to be a retaliatory response to Thursday’s assault on Baidoa – a city that has become a battleground since Laftagaren’s ouster, with local forces under new Southwest leader Adan Madobe and federal troops unable to stop the guerrilla-style attacks that keep hitting the town. “Crossing into a very dangerous territory” Adam Aw Hirsi, Somalia’s former minister of state for environment and climate change, condemned the strike in sharp terms. “This is crossing into a very dangerous territory. I do not think the decision to initiate this attack was wise,” he said. He went further, warning that the episode could set off a cycle of retaliation across Somalia’s fractured political map: “If it is confirmed that foreign drones (Somalia has none) at the behest of @TheVillaSomalia attacked a general’s residence in Dollow, give it less than a year before you hear a drone belonging to an FMS or a clan in hinterland Somalia has struck a foreign embassy in Mogadishu.” “Foreigners involved in this need to reassess,” he added. “Somalis are a tough nut to scare. And you are not without competition in this game. Calculate the benefit of one man’s one-day thrill against the alienation of an entire people and squandering their goodwill.” Jubaland points to a Turkish drone, alleges war crime Jubaland State, which administers Dolow, said the strike was carried out by a Turkish drone. The regional administration described the act as a war crime and said it illustrates the dangerous direction in which President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Turkey are jointly steering Somalia. Jubaland – which is at odds with Mogadishu and has repeatedly clashed with federal forces – said Turkey cannot position itself as part of international efforts to resolve Somalia’s political crisis while conducting such strikes, and it called on international stakeholders to intervene urgently before the fallout unravels the broader political process. Former presidents accuse Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of reckless force Former Somali Presidents Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and Mohamed Abdullahi Farmajo both condemned the attack. They accused President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of using reckless force through foreign powers to pressure his opponents, characterizing the strike as part of a pattern of assassination attempts against political rivals. Mogadishu distances itself, cites explosives inside the house The federal government distanced itself from the air raid, saying an initial investigation indicates the blast was triggered by explosives planted inside the house. It did not say whether Turkey carried out the attack. Turkey itself has not commented on the allegations. What residents heard and saw Despite Mogadishu’s denial of a drone strike, residents in Dolow told local media they heard the sound of a drone and saw a flash of light in the sky before a missile, apparently fired from above, struck the ground with a loud bang. They said the drone’s sound was heard again after the strike. The strike reportedly targeted with precision the room where General Mahad usually sleeps. He was not inside the room when it was hit. Part of a wider pattern of accusations against Ankara Turkey has faced mounting accusations in recent months of siding unreservedly with President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud in his political disputes, a departure from what had long been an international norm under which partners supported Mogadishu on counterterrorism but stayed out of its politicians’ internal disagreements. Ankara has been accused of carrying out deadly drone strikes against Southwest Darwish forces near Baidoa. It has also been linked to suicide drone strikes on buildings housing former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire, which came under attack from federal government forces during two days of fighting in Mogadishu in early June. Turkey was further accused of killing 14 civilians in Puntland State under the stated justification of an anti-piracy operation. Ankara has not commented on any of these accusations. Analysts warn Somalia risks becoming a foreign battleground Somali analysts and politicians say the country could soon become a proxy battleground for foreign powers, and that it would not come as a surprise if international partners aligned with various regional states began launching their own drone strikes on government offices in Mogadishu – now that Turkey, in their view, has set the precedent. Former Somali intelligence chief Fahad Yasin drew a historical parallel, calling the strike as dangerous a turning point as the 2006 car bomb attack on President Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed in Baidoa – the first such explosive attack on a Somali official. He said Friday’s drone strike marks the first drone attack on a former Somali security official who had served the state for a long time. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com

items.title: SPLM-IO governor says Oyet suspension came ‘directly’ from Machar
items.summary: JUBA — A senior official of South Sudan’s main armed opposition group said on Friday that the suspension of acting chairman Oyet Nathaniel was ordered directly by detained leader Riek Machar, weighing into a leadership dispute that has fractured the movement’s political and military ranks. Dhoal Koryom Lingling, an opposition-appointed governor for Unity State, said […] The post SPLM-IO governor s
items.body:
SPLM-IO Governor of Unity State Dhoal Koryom Lingling. [Photo Courtesy] JUBA — A senior official of South Sudan’s main armed opposition group said on Friday that the suspension of acting chairman Oyet Nathaniel was ordered directly by detained leader Riek Machar, weighing into a leadership dispute that has fractured the movement’s political and military ranks.

Dhoal Koryom Lingling, an opposition-appointed governor for Unity State, said Oyet remains a member of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition (SPLM-IO) despite the suspension and could resume his duties if he accepts the decision.

“The reason why I am speaking to the media is because I know where this order is coming from. Oyet appointed me as governor, by the way,” Koryom said in recorded statements on Friday morning.

“If I thought the way you do, I could speak the way you do. But the truth is that Oyet was suspended directly by the chairman (Riek Machar). If you are not aware of that, you should seek that information,” Koryom said.

Koryom did not explain how Machar, who has been held in detention since March 2025, communicated the decision or specify when it was issued.

Under the movement’s official leadership structure, Machar remains chairman and commander-in-chief, while Oyet serves as his deputy. Oyet has been exercising acting leadership responsibilities during Machar’s detention.

“Oyet has not been expelled from the movement. He is still a member,” Koryom said. “If he respects the chairman’s decision, he will return to his duties as deputy chairman and acting chairman.”

The comments add new complexity to a leadership crisis that erupted publicly this week after Oyet suspended interim Secretary-General Regina Joseph Kaba and seven other senior officials, accusing them of misconduct and attempting to undermine his authority.

Oyet said the suspensions were disciplinary measures authorized under the group’s constitution and internal regulations. He accused several members of the Political Bureau of attempting to interfere with the movement’s constitutional order and destabilize its leadership.

Kaba rejected Oyet’s authority to suspend her and issued a counter-directive suspending him as deputy chairman and acting chairman. She also instructed the movement’s political, military, financial, and administrative structures to disregard directives or appointments issued by Oyet.

The dispute has since spread to the SPLA-IO military command.

Senior military commanders meeting this week endorsed the Political Bureau’s resolutions and recognized Kaba as Acting Interim Deputy Chair, while reaffirming Lt. Gen. Peter Thok as the sole Acting Chief of General Staff, according to a statement by the SPLA-IO spokesman.

The command said that directives from “the commander-in-chief” must be respected and implemented. While the statement did not mention Machar by name in that context, its reference to the commander-in-chief appeared to suggest that the decisions had Machar’s backing.

The conflicting decisions have raised questions over who holds political and military authority within the movement while Machar remains unable to lead directly.

Koryom’s assertion that Machar personally authorized Oyet’s suspension could prove significant, as rival factions continue to declare loyalty to Machar while contesting who holds the authority to run the movement in his absence.

Sudans Post could not independently verify whether Machar had personally communicated or approved Oyet’s suspension.

items.title: M23 Rebels Killed As Congolese Army Recaptures South Kivu Towns
items.summary: The clashes are still ongoing in many towns in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The post M23 Rebels Killed As Congolese Army Recaptures South Kivu Towns appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: At least 23 armed fighters have been killed in intense fighting between the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the M23/AFC rebel group. The clashes are still ongoing in the town of Masango and surrounding areas in South Kivu province. Congolese forces announced on Thursday, Sep. 3, that the national army recaptured Masango, Ruhua, and Rubarati after defeating M23/AFC rebels and their Twirwaneho allies in the Hauts Plateaux of Mwenga in South Kivu. Reagan Mbuyi Kalonji, the army spokesperson for Operation Sukola 2 in South Kivu, said these major advances resulted from serious military operations in the zones. “Following our major response against the terrorist coalition of the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) and their allies of the M23, Twirwaneho and Red Tabara in the Hauts Plateaux of Uvira and Fizi, the FARDC have neutralised 23 rebels, 11 others surrendered, and several weapons were recovered,” Reagan said. During the course of operations carried out in Malimba, Masango, Ruhua and Rubarat, the army declared having killed 15 combatants of the M23-Twirwaneho coalition, while six others surrendered before being taken to Uvira. Violent clashes have intensified between the M23 and the Congolese forces in Uvira. The country’s army has said that many rebels have since withdrawn toward Kashongo and Magunda, two strategic localities, allowing the national armed forces to reinforce their positions in the Minembwe region. The army has also claimed it has recaptured several towns and villages from the M23/AFC rebels, including Kamimbi, Nagishashu and Irumba in the Basimunyaka-Sud area. During fighting in the area, eight rebel combatants were killed, and five others surrendered. However, a mass grave was discovered in Masango, where civilians killed by the rebels were buried during the occupation of the town by a rebel coalition, led by the M23 armed group and allegedly supported by Rwanda. items.title: The Children Forced into Street Labour in Chad
items.summary: The precarious situations that many families and their children face in urban centres of Chad are pushing school-age children, who remain at home due to poverty, into street labour and hawking as a means of survival. The post The Children Forced into Street Labour in Chad appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: Idrissa Mahamat navigates the harsh realities of life as a child vendor, selling sachet water under the scorching sun of the bustling Taradona market in the Republic of Chad . Like him, many children are forced into the streets due to family crises, unplanned pregnancies, and abandonment by their parents. Many of these children lack any familial support, compelling them to fend for themselves in a struggle for survival. The harsh conditions that lead to their circumstances often leave them vulnerable and alone, forcing them to confront the challenges of adulthood far too early, locals say. Amid economic hardship and insecurity, a disturbing cycle of vulnerability is taking root, as children are forced into street labour in N’Djamena, the capital of Chad. Driven by poverty and neglect, school-age children face threats of violence and exploitation. In the neighbourhoods and markets of the Chadian capital, it is common to see minors carrying buckets full of sachet water on their heads, searching for customers for their goods. They navigate the streets, motor parks, and bus stations. “The price of the water sachets I sell varies between 25 and 50 FCFA, and on good days, I can sell between one and three buckets full of sachet water and make a profit of about 1,000 FCFA (about US$2), which I hand over to my parents to add to what they have to use in taking care of our family,” nine-year-old Idrissa told HumAngle. As child labour becomes a common phenomenon in Chad, parents and locals in the country’s capital told HumAngle that the largest cause of this scourge is “irresponsible parenting” and carelessness of some guardians and child carers. “Difficult times, divorces, unwanted pregnancies, forced marriages or sometimes the death of parents explain why some of these children find themselves in the situations in which they are,” says a local social worker in Chad, who simply gave their name as Sussane. Tchinduebe Joseph, a father of four, says that after giving birth, many young mothers find themselves alone, struggling to care for both themselves and their newborns. With their partners unwilling to shoulder their share of the burden, these women are often left with no choice but to fend for themselves, sometimes even being pushed out into the streets to survive. At least one in every two school-age children is not enrolled in school, totalling approximately three million children outside the education system in Chad, according to a report by the United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund (UNICEF). The situation seems to have established societal imbalances driving some children into armed groups, while unparented girls face increased risk of rape and sexual exploitation due to their living conditions. The UN agency reports that the abandonment of these minors reflects poorly on Chadian society and families. However, the precarious situations that many families and their children face in urban centres of Chad are pushing school-age children, who remain at home due to poverty, into street labour and hawking as a means of survival. A top official of the N’Djamena City Council in Chad, who asked not to be named in this report, stressed the importance of parental responsibility. Disturbed by the growing number of unparented children in the country, the official quoted a poignant Ivorian adage, saying, “The child has to be fed until he/she grows teeth, and in turn, that child will eventually care for you when you lose your own teeth.” He noted that nurturing and supporting children lays a foundation for mutual care and reciprocity in later life. “In this 21st century, when money is indispensable for survival, poverty within most families and most communities in Chad has been wreaking havoc on normal family life. Even children are not exempted from this unfortunate reality as most of them are being forced into the streets in search of money to supplement the low incomes of their parents,” the official added. UNICEF, on its part, says that children have a right to health, potable water, sufficient food, as well as education as they grow. The child has to be protected against violence, maltreatment, exploitation and armed conflicts while benefiting from a safe home and leisure. The post The Children Forced into Street Labour in Chad appeared first on HumAngle .

items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro departed Hargeisa on Thursday for a working visit to the United States, part of an effort to present the self-declared republic as an emerging power of geoeconomic and geosecurity value to Washington and other Western capitals, with particular emphasis on the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint. Officials said Irro will make a stopover in the United Arab Emirates en route to the US. The Somaliland leader is expected to pitch his territory’s importance to Washington on two fronts: its rare earth mineral deposits and its proximity to Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint, a position officials believe could support a US military footing there and help counter threats from Houthi rebels. Somalia’s federal government has moved in parallel, dispatching a delegation led by Deputy Prime Minister Salah Jama on a counter-diplomacy push aimed at undercutting Irro’s Washington trip. The rival missions have drawn attention to the family ties binding the two camps. “For those who don’t know – Jama is actually from Somaliland and Irro’s kin,” said Rashid Abdi, a Horn of Africa analyst at Sahan Research. “Fascinating diplomacy,” Abdi added. items.body: Taemo Hadish is a farmer in Haweleti, in Raya Zebo, Tigray region. She says her cattle have become too weak to move because of a lack of fodder, while the farmland she relies on to feed her family have failed to grow. “We have not seen rain for the whole year,” she says. “Our animals are dying because there is nothing for them to eat.” The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has warned that parts of Ethiopia could experience below-average rainfall during the June–September rainy season as El Niño conditions develop. In northern Ethiopia, particularly Tigray, conflict-related disruptions to farming seasons have left 21 woredas at high risk of severe food insecurity, with 2.45 million people in need of emergency food assistance. Similar conditions are being reported in neighbouring Afar, where livestock are also dying as the drought worsens. According to a July FAO report, more than 18,000 livestock have died in Yaqer locality, Afar region, due to shortages of water and fodder. Farmers and woreda officials interviewed by the BBC say farmers in three woredas in Tigray region are struggling because of delayed rains linked to El Niño. The weather patterns have caused drought in the southern, south-eastern and central zones, while some woredas that received rainfall have experienced heavy hailstorms and flooding. In its May seasonal forecast, the Ethiopian Meteorology Institute warned that parts of southern and eastern Tigray, North and South Wollo, Afar and eastern Ethiopia were likely to receive below-average rainfall. It also forecast dry conditions in northern and eastern parts of the country in August. “We have never experienced a drought like this. There has not been enough rain, and we are going through a very difficult year,” says Alem Misgana, who lives in Alitena, in the Eastern Zone. Article in Amharic. items.title: Laftagaren forces attack Somali army positions in Baidoa again
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Heavy fighting erupted in Baidoa on Thursday after forces loyal to ousted Southwest State President Abdiasis Laftagaren attacked the city from multiple directions, seizing two federal army bases on its outskirts before entering the town and engaging government troops in fierce gun battles that lasted for hours. Laftagaren’s Darwish forces entered Baidoa […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Heavy fighting erupted in Baidoa on Thursday after forces loyal to ousted Southwest State President Abdiasis Laftagaren attacked the city from multiple directions, seizing two federal army bases on its outskirts before entering the town and engaging government troops in fierce gun battles that lasted for hours. Laftagaren’s Darwish forces entered Baidoa early in the morning, according to a spokesman for the forces, who said they would continue fighting until the last federal soldier leaves the region and control of the region is fully restored to its people. The forces later withdrew from the city, bringing the fighting to an end. Southwest State Information Minister Nur Sidow told reporters in Baidoa after the fighting that those who had attacked the city were Al-Shabaab , and said the assault had begun with suicide car bombs. The Somali federal government made a similar claim last month after Laftagaren’s forces launched another attack on Baidoa. Regional authorities and the federal government have yet to provide any tangible evidence for the assertion that the attackers were Al-Shabaab. The latest fighting left multiple people dead and caused other casualties, although there are no official figures. Among those killed was the commander of the personal guards of current Southwest leader Adan Madobe. Isaq Abdulle, commander of the Somali army’s 8th Brigade of the 60th Division, sustained serious injuries. Baidoa was once a relatively peaceful town under Laftagaren, but it has become a battleground since he was toppled. The repeated attacks by his forces have exposed the inability of the federal government and its Southwest allies to defend the city, even after thousands of troops were deployed there since March, analysts say. The latest assault highlights the continuing security crisis in Baidoa, where recurrent fighting has challenged the federal government’s control of the Southwest State capital. items.title: Sudan’s Sovereignty Council chief inspects army's readiness in Blue Nile State amid escalating clashes with RSF
items.summary: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's visit comes amid escalating clashes between army, Raid Support Forces in Blue Nile State
items.body:
The chairman of Sudan’s Sovereign Council, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, inspected the readiness of the army on Wednesday in Blue Nile state in southeastern Sudan.

The visit comes amid escalating clashes in the state between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N).

In a statement, the army’s 4th infantry division said that Burhan, who also commands the Sudanese army, visited the city of Damazin, the state capital and the headquarters of the division.

It added that Burhan inspected the division’s forces and assessed their combat readiness and preparedness to carry out their assigned missions.

He was also briefed on the security and operational situation in the region, according to the statement.

Burhan stressed “the need to raise levels of preparedness and vigilance and strengthen discipline and combat readiness," according to the statement.

He also called for “continuing to carry out missions in accordance with military plans and directives."

Burhan also inspected the military hospital in Damazin, where he was briefed on the conditions of wounded soldiers and patients, and the hospital’s operations.

He affirmed the army command’s commitment to its personnel and to providing them with the necessary care.

The statement quoted 4th Infantry Division Commander Maj. Gen. Ismail al-Tayeb, who said Burhan’s visit “enhanced their readiness to carry out their missions.”

“The division’s forces are fully prepared to perform their military duties, secure the region and protect civilians,” he said.

He added that the division was ready to “continue implementing the plans and directives issued by the command.”

Burhan’s visit comes amid rapidly developing military developments in Blue Nile state.

On Tuesday, the first contingent of joint forces from armed movements allied with the army arrived in Blue Nile state.

On Saturday, the army announced that it deployed an elite brigade affiliated with the General Intelligence Service to the battlefield in the Bakori axis in the state.

The RSF announced Friday that it seized the Bakori and Sarkam military bases southeast of Damazin.

The army also announced last Thursday that it had shot down a “hostile” drone in Blue Nile state after it crossed the border from Ethiopia.

It said it was the third drone it had announced shooting down within a week.

In addition to Blue Nile and the Darfur region in western Sudan, clashes have been ongoing in the three Kordofan states -- North, West and South Kordofan -- between the army and the RSF since Oct. 25.

Sudan has been witnessing a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, which has killed tens of thousands and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Armed militias seized centers designated for voter registration in Beledweyne on Tuesday, as Somalia’s electoral commission set September 30 for Hirshabelle municipal and parliamentary elections, intensifying opposition to the planned vote, Caasimada Online news website reported on Tuesday. Some of the militias, speaking to local media, said they oppose the elections being conducted by the government-appointed electoral commission. They said they would not accept a vote in which only one favored candidate is allowed to contest while all other candidates are banned, arguing that the process mirrors such an arrangement. The Somali federal government has not yet taken any action against the militias. The seizure comes as Hawadle clan politicians strongly oppose the planned Hirshabelle election, saying the process is not fair. They are also demanding their turn at the presidency of the Hirshabelle regional administration. The competing objections have placed the planned elections under heightened political tension in Beledweyne, where the seizure of the registration centers has directly disrupted locations designated for the electoral process. The militias’ opposition centers on what they describe as a process that favors one candidate while excluding others, while Hawadle politicians are challenging the fairness of the Hirshabelle election and pressing for their turn at the regional presidency. With the electoral commission having scheduled the Hirshabelle municipal and parliamentary elections for September 30, the dispute over the process remains unresolved, while the Somali federal government has yet to take action against the militias. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com

items.title: Violent Clashes Stall School Reopenings in DRC
items.summary: Since at least 2025, hundreds of schoolchildren have been denied access to schools and educational facilities due to the violent clashes between the rebel groups and state forces. The resurgence of the Ebola virus has worsened the situation, as schools tried to reopen amid the disease outbreak. The post Violent Clashes Stall School Reopenings in DRC appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: Violent clashes between the Congolese armed forces and the M23 rebels have disrupted school reopenings in several localities in North Kivu in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). As the 2026-2027 academic year begins, schools have not yet reopened in several rural areas of the region, particularly in the Bankindi, Banamulema, and Balindu communities of the Kisimba tribal group. Just before the school year was set to begin, many families were forced to flee their homes to escape the intense fighting between the armed groups, particularly the Wazalendo militia, and the M23/AFC rebels in the region. Parents, students, and teachers have sought refuge to avoid the crossfire. Some families have taken shelter in the bushes, while others have relocated to towns like Pinga and Kalembe. The situation is severely compromising the normal reopening of school activities. For the displaced families, the immediate priority is survival, especially since they lack the means to pay school fees for their children. “We escaped with our children without carrying along our belongings. Today, we do not even know where we will sleep or what we will eat,” a parent taking refuge with his family in Pinga told HumAngle. “Under these conditions, it is difficult for us to think about school fees, uniforms or other school needs for our children. We very much wish for peace to return so that our children can return to school.” Some schools in Pinga have started admitting children of displaced families from zones affected by the fighting. A senior official from Kabeza Secondary School in Pinga, whose name is withheld for safety reasons, stated that the influx of students creates space issues, as the school must accommodate additional students from war-affected areas. “We are forced to welcome children from displaced families in order to enable them to continue their education. However, admitting them is not easy because some come without school requirements and their parents do not have the means to meet their needs. We demand assistance so that these children are not abandoned because of the war,” the official said. Faced with this situation, authorities in the education sector of the Walikale 3 sub-division are encouraging displaced parents to enrol their children in schools in their refuge zones, notably in Pinga and Kalembe, so they can continue schooling. Families hiding in bushes with their children, lacking access to schools, subsistence means, and essential services, are compromising their children’s educational futures. Since at least 2025, hundreds of schoolchildren have been denied access to schools and educational facilities due to the violent clashes between the rebel groups and state forces. The resurgence of the Ebola virus has worsened the situation, as schools tried to reopen amid the disease outbreak. The post Violent Clashes Stall School Reopenings in DRC appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: Kidnapping on the Rise Near Cameroon’s Border with Nigeria
items.summary: The surge in kidnapping near Cameroon’s border with Nigeria coincides with several ongoing crises in the region. The post Kidnapping on the Rise Near Cameroon’s Border with Nigeria appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: A report from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA) has revealed that over 300 persons were kidnapped by terrorists in the Far North region of Cameroon during April, May, and June of 2026. In the same timeframe in 2025, 141 abductions were reported, which is a staggering 118 per cent increase in kidnappings. The recent report shows a serious decline in the region’s security landscape in the second quarter of 2026. During this period, 72 people were killed, and 48 were injured, which actually reflects a 6.5 per cent decrease in fatalities compared to the previous year, when 77 civilians lost their lives. The UNOCHA report stresses that understanding the worsening security situation in Far North Cameroon requires more than just looking at casualty numbers. Compared to the latter half of 2025, there were 167 more kidnappings, suggesting that abductions have become the major form of violence affecting communities near the Nigerian border. Beyond the loss of lives, terrorist operations in the region seem to have established a pervasive climate of fear, limiting movement and undermining the livelihood of local communities. The report states that such violence can lead to new displacements as people flee to areas deemed safer. For humanitarian organisations, the ongoing insecurity complicates efforts to deliver assistance to those in need. The report also noted a resurgence of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) in the Logone-et-Chari division, with two such incidents occurring between April and June this year. While the limited occurrences of IEDs do not definitively indicate a sustained reduction in violence, they add to the potential risks faced by residents and humanitarian workers, especially during periods of displacement in violence-affected areas. This surge in kidnappings coincides with several ongoing crises in the region. The UNOCHA report mentions new population displacements, a worsening measles outbreak, the emergence of cholera cases, and ongoing food insecurity. The post Kidnapping on the Rise Near Cameroon’s Border with Nigeria appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: Somalia NSA confirms troops crossed into Ethiopia region
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Aways Haji Yusuf, on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that an undisclosed number of Somali National Army (SNA) troops who recently completed a Saudi Arabia-funded training program in Hanaanbure, Galmudug, have crossed into Ethiopia’s Somali region. Yusuf said the soldiers, who had undergone more than a year […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Aways Haji Yusuf, on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that an undisclosed number of Somali National Army (SNA) troops who recently completed a Saudi Arabia-funded training program in Hanaanbure, Galmudug, have crossed into Ethiopia’s Somali region. Yusuf said the soldiers, who had undergone more than a year of training, were granted leave to visit their families and that the federal government is aware of their presence in the region for that purpose. “If there are other issues, we will let you (media) know,” Yusuf told reporters. Defection Reports Preceded the Admission The confirmation comes days after multiple Somali media outlets, including outlets based in Ethiopia’s Somali region, reported that dozens of soldiers – part of a cohort of 3,000 trained at Hananbure – had defected and were subsequently captured by regional forces before being taken to Jigjiga. Reported figures for the number involved have varied widely across outlets, with some citing 300, others 180, and others as high as 900. None of these figures has been independently confirmed, and it remains unclear whether the soldiers defected or were simply on approved leave to visit their families, as the government maintains. Analyst: Admission “Likely to Generate More Questions” A Nairobi-based Horn of Africa analyst with Sahan Research described the National Security Adviser’s admission as “refreshing and commendable, but likely to generate more questions.” “Did Somalia recruit forces from the Somali Regional State of Ethiopia with permission from regional and federal authorities? If not, how will Addis Ababa respond?” the analyst asked. A Backdrop of Strained Ties The episode unfolds against a backdrop of strained relations between Mogadishu and Addis Ababa in recent years, with the two governments aligned to separate geopolitical camps. Ethiopia has increasingly sided with the United Arab Emirates, including in its support for the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, while Somalia has increasingly aligned itself with Saudi Arabia and Turkey. items.title: 22,000 displaced by fighting in Sudan’s Blue Nile state in last week: UN
items.summary: Agency says civilians fleeing violence in Geissan district have sought safety in several areas, including state capital Ed Damazine
items.body:
About 22,000 people have been displaced from Sudan’s Blue Nile state in the last week as fighting intensified in the Geissan district, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said Tuesday.

OCHA said in a statement that continued violence is putting civilians at risk and forcing thousands to flee their homes.

“In Blue Nile State, local authorities report that nearly 22,000 people may have been displaced in the past seven days due to escalating fighting in the locality of Geissan,” it said.

The statement said that “many are sheltering in schools or have fled to other areas, including towards the state capital, Ed Damazine.”

The Geissan Emergency Room, a local aid body, said Sunday that nearly 20,000 people had fled the area of Medina 12 in the Geissan district because of the fighting and worsening security conditions.

Blue Nile has seen a new escalation in the last two days after the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North launched attacks in several areas of the state.

OCHA also said attacks on Saturday on villages north and northwest of El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, caused casualties and displaced civilians, amid reports that civilian property and livestock were looted.

“In West Darfur State, civilians were reportedly killed and injured when a drone strike hit a fuel market in Adekong, near the border with Chad, last Thursday. The attack also damaged civilian property,” it said.

OCHA renewed its demand for all parties to the conflict “to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, respect international humanitarian law, and allow humanitarian organizations to operate safely and independently.”

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Monday that 450 people were displaced from the village of al-Qardud Abu Zeid in the al-Rahad district of North Kordofan because of deteriorating security in a single day.

Alongside Blue Nile and Darfur, fighting has continued since Oct. 25 in Sudan’s three Kordofan states -- North Kordofan, West Kordofan and South Kordofan -- between the army and the RSF.

Sudan has been at war between the army and the RSF since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

items.title: Terrorism forces 57 primary schools to shut in Nigeria’s Borno, 80 students remain captive: Official
items.summary: Soldiers have been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes.
items.body:
At least 57 primary schools are currently not functioning in Nigeria’s northeastern Borno State due to insecurity, while about 80 students abducted during attacks on schools remain in captivity, according to local education authorities.

The situation was disclosed by Fasuma Askira, education secretary of Askira-Uba Local Government Area, where only 56 of the 113 primary schools are currently operating.

On May 15, terrorists attacked Mussa Central Primary School and abducted dozens of children. Although the exact number remains disputed, the Borno State Government has more recently put the number of missing pupils at about 44.

On June 29, insurgents attacked Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were sitting for a National Examinations Council examination. Some students were subsequently rescued, but 36 students and a teacher remained in captivity.

Combining the latest government estimate from Mussa with the verified Lassa figure puts the number of students still in captivity at about 80.

As of Aug. 31, the children abducted from Mussa had spent 108 days in captivity, while the Lassa students had been held for 63 days.

Simon Waindu, whose daughter is among the Lassa students, said none of the children had returned and that families had received no information about their rescue.

Meanwhile, authorities have closed schools in communities affected by insecurity. Authorities have also proposed the deployment of community vigilantes around schools when classes resume, while soldiers have been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes.

The latest developments come after Anadolu reported in June that terrorists abducted six women and two babies near the scene of a school attack in Borno state.

The incident occurred shortly after suspected insurgents attacked Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were taking examinations, further highlighting the vulnerability of civilians around schools in the conflict-affected region.

Nigeria's northeastern states have faced more than a decade of insurgency, with Boko Haram and ISWAP among the armed groups responsible for attacks, abductions and displacement.

The continued captivity of students and closure of schools raise concerns over the long-term educational consequences of the conflict, particularly for children in communities already affected by displacement and poverty.

items.title: Displacement and the Right to Vote: Addressing the Exclusion of Nigeria’s IDPs in the 2027 GeneralElections
items.summary: Introduction Between April 2025 and June 2026, over 2.3 million internally displaced people (IDPs) were identified by the International Organisation for Migration’s 51st DTM Site Assessment. items.body: Introduction Between April 2025 and June 2026, over 2.3 million internally displaced people (IDPs) were identified by the International Organisation for Migration’s 51st DTM Site Assessment. The data highlights a 2% increase from Round 50 of the assessment. The number represents a population of Nigerians covered by the constitution and, specifically, the National Policy on IDPs to restore their rights, agency and dignity. Mostly uprooted by long-running conflicts, HumAngle found that IDPs across various communities are being pushed outside the map of the 2027 electoral processes, denying them the opportunity to exercise their rights and exposing systemic failure and neglect. What’s New? HumAngle travelled to rural communities and town centres where IDPs are hosted. Across communities in Adamawa, Borno and Katsina states, there is a pattern of recurring barriers to IDPs’ electoral participation . These include incomplete voter registration exercises, difficulty replacing or transferring Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs), limited voter education, lack of information about registration procedures, the cost and insecurity associated with travelling to original polling units, and declining confidence in the electoral process. Key findings HumAngle identifies a policy gap in the management of IDP challenges. The National Policy on IDPs says all rights contained in the Nigerian constitution and humanitarian instruments are to be enjoyed by IDPs. Yet, this has not been the case across many IDP camps. There are practical barriers to voter registration. Often, due to logistical failure to reach IDP camps and the poor implementation of the Independent National Electoral Commission’s IDPs Voting Regulations . IDPs have demonstrated their desire for inclusion and participation in electoral processes, with many first-time voters hoping to be enrolled in the voter register. Voter education and information gaps in IDP communities persist. IDPs with lost or damaged voter cards do not know how to get a replacement, while INEC’s online self-service option is ineffective due to the digital gaps in IDP and conflict-affected communities. No polling infrastructure within IDP camps. Where field visits were conducted, IDPs who have their voter cards have to go back to communities they fled to vote, further exposing them to the risks of harm. Why does it matter? Inclusion is crucial for a constitutional democracy and a nation attempting to heal from radicalisation. In this context, it restores confidence in the state and gives agency to citizens who are in their most vulnerable state. Invariably, this enhances recovery, and restores a sense of belonging for a population that seems to exist in limbo. Social recovery does not work in isolation. It has to be a whole approach, and INEC’s voter registration and participation in elections by IDPs is part of this larger process of recovery and agency-giving for IDPs. The integrity of electoral processes is only intact when no one feels excluded. What can be done INEC should create a special window urgently to regularise IDPs, register those of voting age with a special target to first-time voters across identified communities. This will enable the completion of registration, enrolment of new voters, and replacement of lost or damaged cards ahead of the 2027 elections. INEC should revamp its voter education campaign through collaboration with the National Orientation Agency and Local Government Community Development Departments to reach IDPs with clear and needed voter education and information. Civil society and the media should continue independent monitoring and reporting on voter registration and election-related exercises to keep issues visible to policymakers and the public. Humanitarian and camp management actors should integrate voter education activities within camp programmes to bridge awareness gaps. They should also leverage existing camp leadership structures to coordinate with INEC, schedule visits and follow up. The National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons (NCFRMI) should review the National IDP Policy and develop a complementary national framework that elaborately operationalises how the participation of IDPs in elections should henceforth be governed. Conclusion The 2027 general election is near, and IDPs, especially first-time voters, are enthusiastic and hopeful to participate in a civic exercise. The constitution granted them the right; the laws and policies empower them with the opportunity, but the system is locking them out. This clash between policy and practice has consequences. It disenfranchises and breeds national grievances where healing, recovery and agency should take centre. INEC and all relevant stakeholders have a role to reverse the dying hope for inclusion, stronger democracy and electoral integrity. Further reading Nigeria’s Displaced Communities Risk Being Shut Out of Elections, https://www.humanglemedia.com/nigerias-displaced-communities-risk-being-shut-out-of-elections Regulations for Voting by Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), https://www.inecnigeria.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/REGULATIONS.pdf Acknowledgment This policy brief was made possible through the dedication of a talented team of professionals, led by Abdussamad Ahmad Yusuf, for the research, analysis, and drafting of this document. The post Displacement and the Right to Vote: Addressing the Exclusion of Nigeria’s IDPs in the 2027 GeneralElections appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: Italy Expands Police Training Support for Somalia
items.summary: Talyaaniga ayaa Muqdisho ku shaaciyay qorshe lagu xoojinayo iskaashiga amni ee Soomaaliya, iyadoo diiradda la saarayo tababarka booliiska, dhismaha hay’adaha amniga iyo ka hortagga xagjirnimada.
